utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Tuesday. I would first like to greet Mr. Praljak, and I would also like to greet the accused, as well as the counsels, and Mr. Stringer and all the members of the OTP. I shall not forget Mr. Coric, and I hope that he gets better soon, because as you are aware, he will not be in this courtroom for quite a while. I would also like to greet everyone who is assisting us, the court reporter, the interpreters, as well as everybody else in this courtroom. We shall resume the cross-examination of Mr. Coric [as interpreted], represented by his counsel, and I give her the floor immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Praljak. Good morning to all. At the beginning of my cross-examination today, I would like to go back to something that the President asked yesterday, and that is why I have distributed a new binder, in a bid to shed more light on a particular situation. May the binder please be handed to the witness. It consists of a mere two documents. I will try to use these two documents to demonstrate my point, and demonstrate it through the examination of Mr. Praljak. Otherwise, I would, myself, be testifying, which is certainly not my intention. Mr. Praljak, first of all, may I ask you to look at the names of both these documents. The first document is 2D00906. This is the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Mr. Praljak, are you aware of this law and its existence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we please move on to 2D00907. Mr. Praljak, is this the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the first document and look at Article 7 of that document. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 7 reads: "Provisions of the general part of this Code are applicable to all criminal acts defined in the laws of the federation, republics, and autonomous provinces." Mr. Praljak, you were a citizen of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, were you not? Therefore, what I would like to know is whether you knew of the existence of criminal acts defined by the federal laws as well as those criminal acts defined by the laws of the republics and autonomous provinces, as stated in this Article.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now please go to Article 104 of that same law. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 of Article 104 reads: "Yugoslav criminal law applies to anybody who has committed a criminal act on the territory of the SFRY." Were you aware of this, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we now please go to Article 110 of that same law, paragraph 1 of that Article, which reads: "Criminal codes of republics and autonomous provinces apply to anybody who, on the territory of the republic or autonomous province, commits a criminal act for which the law provides a punishment, regardless of where he is tried for the act." Mr. Praljak, were you aware of the existence of the Criminal Code of the republics and autonomous provinces that were applied in relation to crimes committed in those same republics or autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. In relation to the first Article, that the law being applied -- the local law being applied whenever a crime is committed in a particular area, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to our following document, 2D00907. Article 3, please. Article 3 reads -- this is the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Article 3 reads: "In the application of the provisions of this law, and provisions of other laws of the republics that contain provisions of the criminal law, provisions of the general part of the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are also to be applied." Mr. Praljak, do you know what this means and were you aware of this? Do you agree with me that this means that at the same time, both these laws are applied that we are looking at, each in its own respective domain?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that written as clearly in Article 3. The Article reads that a certain set of laws applies, but also the general provisions of the Criminal Code. I find this counter-intuitive, because the provisions in relation to the first law and then the other law are not specified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Praljak. The Chamber is aware of the law behind this, and they will be looking into that. I do not expect you to interpret these regulations. All I want to confirm is that you, as a citizen, were aware of both these laws. We shall be dwelling on this, but let us for a moment go back to the document where it all began, and that is in my binder number 2, 3D03027. It is the binder that you have in front of you. While we're looking for that document, Mr. Praljak, and this is something that the Prlic Defence has been using, you are aware of the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HZ-HB adopted both these laws through their own provisions, are you not? You didn't hear me?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I knew that the laws were adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you located this document, 3D03027?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us try to look what there is right after number 1. It reads: "Criminal reports for violent behaviour, as described under Article 204, paragraph 2, of the adopted KZSRBH, Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, were filed against Ranko Milicevic, Branko Milicevic, Davor Trogolic [phoen] ...," and so on and so forth. Mr. Praljak, what about this abbreviation, KZSRBH? That should read "Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina"; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on for a moment to the 907 document, it is the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 2D0907. We saw that this is a document by Colonel Blaskic about violent behaviour. Could you please locate Article 204 in the last document, the law of the socialist -- the Criminal Code of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and tell me as soon as you've got it. It reads "Violent Behaviour," and what the Article describes is that particular criminal offence. Mr. Praljak, am I right in stating that the criminal offence in relation to which a criminal report was filed in D03027 is in relation to the crime described in Article 204, defined here as violent behaviour?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Praljak. You can leave the binder containing the two laws aside for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, counsel has stated that Article 204 had to do with violent behaviour, but while commenting on Article 3 of this law, you asked yourself a series of questions and discover, as things are going along, that you are a legal expert yourself. If I understand correctly, as regards the Criminal Code of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the law is applicable in all the republics, but in each and every republic you could have autonomous laws that could solve -- or that could deal with certain behaviours. Now, when dealing with the refusal to execute an order, which appears in the federal code, Article 204, the JNA has a role that stretches over all the republics. So as far as you are concerned, the behaviour of a JNA soldier who would be positioned in Mostar and who would refuse to execute an order from General Perisic, if we assume this for a moment, would this behaviour be dealt with by Article 204 of the federal code or would it be dealt with by a specific text from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when we deal with a soldier from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The federal law alone, Your Honour. No republican or provincial laws apply to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Let us move along where we left off yesterday. That's in the red binder.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel please speak closer to the microphone. We can't hear counsel properly. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] P03409. I do apologise to the interpreters. I wasn't sufficiently close enough to the microphone. 3409.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a decision to launch a disciplinary investigation, adopted by Commander Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, addressed to the assistant commander for the SIS of Central Bosnia Operations Zone. If we look at the first two paragraphs, they read: "1. I nominate and appoint Mr. Anto Sliskovic to conduct a disciplinary investigation of the 4th Military Police Battalion commander, Mr. Pasko Ljubicic." Your Honours, there's something going on with the transcript. It's not running. Oh, it's running again now. "I nominate and appoint Mr. Anto Sliskovic ..." Paragraph 2: "Task: Establish the factual situation, including a written record of the interview with the perpetrator of disciplinary offence and report accordingly to the superior officer." And then we go on to point 3, which gives the dead-line by which this order is to be carried out. And point 4 says that upon completion of the investigation, the disciplinary file, report and proposal are to be forwarded to the superior officer. At the top of the document, before we see the title "Decision," it says that the decision was passed pursuant to the Code of Military Discipline, and it refers to some articles within that Code. Tell me, please, Mr. Praljak, did you know of cases of this kind, and was this the procedure, in your opinion? Was this procedure in conformity with the Code on Military Discipline to which Colonel Blaskic refers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, of course, did not know about this specific case, and you should always say, Oh, I'll do that, say which document you're going to ask me about, whether it's when I was there, when I was the commander and chief of the Main Staff, and which documents you'd like to hear my comments on about what I knew of the functioning of the overall system of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So yesterday we were looking at a document on discipline, disciplinary measures and disciplinary rules, and disciplinary procedure, in fact, applies to all the members of the armed forces of the HZ-HB. Let me make myself clear. I could have punished, for example, in disciplinary terms, General Petkovic and all the members down the line below General Petkovic in the Main Staff, and I could also discipline the zone commanders, the area commanders. Of course, the area commanders, those of the brigades, battalions, companies and so on, those commanders, of course, punished and discipline their own soldiers, but a disciplinary procedure also applies to the military police battalions and companies and all those who had military ID cards. It wasn't limited to only the military part of the HVO. Now, as far as this is concerned, you have two things here, two points. First of all, the form of the document and the form, well, of the security services, which had assistance of the head of the Department for Security, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I do apologise, but we've already heard all those explanations in response to Ms. Alaburic and Ms. Nozica's questions, and indeed during the examination-in-chief. All I'm interested in is to hear whether, to your -- in your opinion, did Colonel Blaskic act properly and was this in keeping with the rules and regulations and code governing military discipline? That's all I'm interested in. This document does not date back to the times that you were there, but the same provisions and rules held true during your time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Mr. Blaskic considered that Pasko Ljubicic, for example, had violated something that he considered to come under the Code on Military Discipline, then here he asks the assistant SIS commander, which according to establishment terms, he acted properly. He asked that this commander, who was supposed to be in a superior position to the military police, should act in such a way as that after conducting disciplinary investigations, a disciplinary sanction should have been pronounced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we've seen this document and we've seen other documents yesterday, and there's a major point that the counsel of Mr. Coric is trying to bring to light, and it is the following: The military police was reporting to whom? Was it reporting to the brigade commander or was it an autonomous entity, not reporting to the brigade commander? Depending on the answer, the legal or criminal liability according to Article 7.3 will be different, so this is what is at stake here. We have a document before us, drafted by Mr. Blaskic, and it is obvious that he has handed down a decision asking to have a fact-finding mission or to issue a report, so it seems that he has decided to have control over this matter. But I'm going to choose another case. Let's assume that the military police of a brigade, whatever that brigade may be, sees that soldiers are basically distributing watches and wallets that have been stolen from people who were the subject of a military operation, and the military police have several options. They can say, Well, this is war booty, and if it is war booty, then a list should be drafted. There's an entire procedure that you have to go through, and I thank you very much for giving us this information yesterday, for those who were not aware of this. But as you said yesterday, a procedure should be followed, and in that case the military police realises that the soldiers are not following this procedure and that they are basically sharing the booty. My question is the following: Should they start, proprio motu, an investigation, inform the SIS and wait for the SIS to refer it to the military prosecutor and leave the brigade commander in the dark? The other option would be that they could rush to the brigade commander and say, We have seen that some soldiers were basically taking watches, money, wallets, and so on; you have to give us some instruction in order to find out whether we should start an investigation or not. So you see that the situations may be different. So according to you, do you think that the military police -- and I've already asked you the question, but we have to go back to this question, so I'm going to rephrase this. The military police, would they refer or report to the brigade in its daily activities, which is also to make sure that law and order is upheld, or do you think that the brigade commander has no authority over the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, I know that this is a very important issue and has to be fully clarified, and I did do my best to do that. The military police is an autonomous organisation which has its chief, it has its professional component, it is to be found in the military police battalions, divided into companies, and part of the men are to be found in the brigade, which is called the brigade military police. Now, the brigade military police, as far as the brigade commander is concerned or the area commander is concerned, performs his daily duties. He doesn't have to ask permission on a daily basis as to who's going to stand guard over a command post, for example, or a forward command post, or whatever, who will escort a convoy of soldiers up to their positions or from their positions, and the like, or who is going to set up a blockade on a road if an operation is underway, and so on and so forth. So tasks of that kind, as far as the brigade commander is concerned, or the commander of the operations zone, is performed by the military police as their daily tasks, but the military police, with respect to its composition, appointments, the salaries the men receive, and the duties performed by the military police, in those terms the military police is duty-bound to take all steps and action described within their daily tasks, within their tasks generally; that is to say, to take down the particulars of individuals, to take people into custody, to request an investigation, and so on and so forth. And as we're dealing with HVO soldiers in this case, or an officer, or whatever, they have to inform the commander of a brigade, or battalion, or whoever else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I just would like to say that we have a technical hitch in the courtroom. The transcript isn't working properly, or, rather it stopped at 11.22. So we don't want to lose what Mr. Praljak said, although the transcript that we see on our screens is working properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, could you please finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't know what has been recorded and what has not. Everything I hear -- I'm being told that everything is recorded on the transcript that we see on our screens. So as I was saying, that part of the SIS and the military police, according to its establishment and its competence and authority and its duties, was one body, a single body in charge of security. And at the head of that body, there was the assistant head of the Defence Department, or should have been. I don't know why that didn't exist. All we had were the chiefs for the SIS and the military police who, in turn, had to maintain close cooperation in security matters, overall security matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, let me discuss another case even more specific. This is a very important topic, and we don't want to make mistakes. When Judges will have to deliberate on this, they want to have all the information at hand. So say there's a military operation going on in a village called X. It's an operation with orders and everything is done regularly. In the framework of this operation, the brigade commander is asking the military police to do its job, as it usually does. So the military operation is carried out, the enemy is captured, and in this village there are civilians that are hiding in their houses. And then a number of soldiers enter into a house, carry out crimes, for example, let's say they rape a woman. They leave the body in the house, and they just leave the premises and go about their military operation. The military police then enters after them, enters into the village after them, check what is happening, and when they enter into this house they see that there is the body of this woman. It's a civilian, and obviously she was the victim of a crime. But at this very moment, the brigade command is not aware of the fact. He's in his headquarters and he has no idea that anything went on. But the military police has noted that a crime was committed. If the military police decides to do nothing and remains silent, and decide not to report to the brigade commander, nothing will happen, or maybe the military police can decide to carry out an investigations to find out who entered the house and then they report to the brigade commander that a war crime was committed. The brigade commander now is informed. Now, as far as you're concerned, were you ever confronted with this kind of situation? Did you ever run into this similar -- and in the example that I described, what should the military police do and what should the brigade commander do? After an operation of the kind, isn't the brigade commander duty-bound to check whether collateral damage occurred or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander is duty-bound to do something; to check and see if that is at all possible, if there's no fighting going on. Now, that's a question. But if he did learn about something like this having taken place, if he learned about it personally, he's duty-bound to inform the military police about it. Let's look at it this way: If he happened to be fighting, came across a situation of this kind, then pursuant to Article 20 whatever, he's going to secure the location, place two soldiers to stand guard there, and then he's going to wait for the military police to arrive or, rather, the crime section of the military police, to take down the facts on site, and the brigade commander himself does not go any further than that. He just secures the spot. Now, once the military police has established the facts, it launches an investigation against perpetrator or perpetrators unknown, if they are unknown, and it is the SIS that goes on to pursue the perpetrators, and this is when an investigation is actually launched because the person perpetrating the crime --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise sincerely for the interruption, Mr. President. My colleague, Ms. Nozica, was right. A few minutes ago, anyone who's trying to work in e-court with LiveNote is not able to do so, I don't think. I'm getting some nods from around the courtroom, which for those of us who are trying to do that, it's highly frustrating, and I wonder if we could get that fixed while the general continues his testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, I've informed the IT Department and they're currently working on the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll take this technical aspect on board. General Praljak, please continue with your answer. You told us what would happen if the brigade commander was informed of the situation. Now, let's imagine the case where he was not informed. Is he duty-bound to check, himself, that anything happened or is he supposed to just trust the military police, at the risk of not being informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I don't understand your question. How can he take action if he doesn't know about something? He has to receive information either from soldiers -- he must have the basic information, and only once he has the basic information concerning a particular case can he react in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand your surprise. Let's imagine a situation where the brigade commander, the commander of the operational zone, or yourself, as HVO commander, are busy with a number of activities, but that on the field -- but you're not kept abreast of what happened on the field. In the example I gave, you know, let's say that the military police turns a blind eye and decides not to do anything. So my question is the following: Isn't the brigade commander duty-bound to check for himself to make sure that his order was correctly executed and that, for example, there were no civilian casualties, and so forth and so on, or does he just blindly trust the military police, at the risk that the military police could not do the job properly or could decide to hide a number of facts from the military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how precisely to answer this question. For instance, when I was in combat, I verified the facts where I was. This is supposed to be done by the brigade commander if he's taking part in a fight and receives reports that this -- and this has happened, if the SIS has given information. Most frequently, for example, we would receive information that -- in Rama, for instance, it happened to me. The chief of the SIS centre, Luka Markesic, would approach me, and he was a very responsible person in that respect. He would learn of a crime. Most frequently behind the front-line, when there's fighting going on, usually there is no civilians in the area where the two armies clash. And he would tell me, desperate, that he'd learned that something had happened in a certain village. I would ask him, Okay, who committed the crime? Now the chase for that perpetrator begins. But it means to have people within the structures who are working for you. Perpetrators will not volunteer their identity. They did it in the dark, with a mask on. They removed number plates from their vehicle. They're trying to cover up their tracks. But after certain statements are given, identification is organised, or people may blurt out something after drinking in cafes and something will be learned. Investigation, in a case of murder or a rape, takes some time. The commander would be familiar with this because they would be informed along the command line of the SIS and their departments, and investigation starts. And once the prosecution is involved in a certain way, then the commander of the brigade or some other unit has nothing to do with it, doesn't have the time to deal with it. Of course, if they have information, they will furnish it. I see no complication in terms of who does what and what is the respective purview of each structure. What you asked me about, if a brigade commander, military police, or SIS, were to see something and some structures want to white-wall a piece of information or some facts, then they have to report to their superior officer and the superior officer of that military police unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I meant to visit all these issues in good time. His Honour Antonetti pre-empted my endeavours in that respect. I will revisit some of those issues on the basis of some documents in the binder. Let's take a look at document P044 -- P04494.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, on several occasions during your testimony, you answered questions. The number is P04494. On several occasions, you said that operative commanding is one thing, and it's another thing to have a commander positioned in terms of reporting, and this is what you explained in the case of the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at this document. This is a document dated 25th of August, 1993, dating from the period while you were in charge, authored by Tihomir Blaskic again. Mr. Blaskic says that: "Pursuant to Article 34, paragraph 2, of the Bylaw on the Military Forces, and pursuant to the authority of the commander of the OZ Central Bosnia, he appoints as commander of the 3rd Light Assault Battalion Military Police, Mr. Vlado Cosic," date of birth, et cetera, and there's the date of this order. It says that it appears to be addressed to the addressee, to the Main Staff of the HVO, and the PPP. I do not know what it understands for. It's PPP of the OZ SB. Are you familiar with the fact that such situations occurred, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, such cases did occur in the Central Bosnia Operations Zone because Mate Boban, the supreme commander of the armed forces of the HZ-HB, through a particular and special order of his, authorised Tihomir Blaskic, entitling him to appoint brigade commanders and commanders of light assault battalions, because this is more of a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Mr. President, just a clarification for the record, because I think it's an important one. We have in the English transcript that the general has just said that Mr. Boban issued a special order authorising Tihomir Blaskic to appoint brigade commanders, and I see the document relates to a battalion, and I don't know whether there was -- whether it's "brigade commander" is the word the general said or whether there was a translation issue there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, what did you say, exactly? I thought I understood, in French, that Mate Boban had delegated the authority to Blaskic to appoint brigade commanders, whereas normally it was a remit of Mate Boban. Is this what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, and I meant to continue; brigade commanders, battalion commanders, et cetera. And to the best of my knowledge, in that order Colonel Blaskic received authority to execute operative command over military police and the light assault units without seeking permission from Valentin Coric, Bruno Stojic, et cetera. So whether, in that order, there was his entitlement to appoint commanders of light assault battalions, that I do not know, but I do know that he was authorised to appoint and organise the army as it should have been structured according to rules and regulations and to execute operative command in terms of using the military police units in Central Bosnia. Whether he was entitled to appoint commanders of light assault battalions or not, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, what you're saying is not unconsequential. Let's imagine we're in a situation where the commander of the HVO personally notes that one of his subordinates, i.e., Colonel Blaskic here, is directly in contact with Mate Boban and gives himself the authority to appoint whoever he wants, without you having anything to say in this. This means that you, as commander of the HVO, are placed in a delicate situation. Is that the situation you encountered, when it comes to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I wouldn't be placed in an inconvenient situation for the simple reason that Central Bosnia was completely cut off from the rest. It was physically impossible to reach that area to execute control, inspect. People were not known. And in my opinion, Mr. Boban did the right thing. I could not personally appoint brigade commanders, and Mate Boban did the right thing by giving him such authority. Central Bosnia was completely encircled. There was no time for correspondence. The telephones were down. On occasions, he had to react militarily within five minutes, and in such situations it is only logical to delegate authority to somebody to increase military efficiency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I fully understand what you're saying. Unfortunately, the reality of military events does not coincide with international law. Normally, you have a chain of command, with the commander of the HVO and all his subordinates. Now, here you're telling us what probably happened. In reality, we'll see that later, you know, at the end of the cross-examination. But you're developing a case according to which Central Bosnia was fully encircled, that there was a direct connection between Blaskic and Boban without anyone like you, General Petkovic, or maybe Mr. Stojic or Mr. Coric, having anything to say in this, because the situation was an emergency, and because of this emergency there was a direct chain that had been set up between Blaskic and Boban. I can understand that, you know, when it comes to military operations are concerned. The question now is whether the law should be applied or not in this kind of situation. If events occur in Central Bosnia, for example, war crimes, and the normal chain of command is totally bypassed, Mr. Bypass [as interpreted] is directly in contact with Mr. Boban, and senior officers can say, Well, I wasn't told about anything, I wasn't kept informed, I wasn't aware of anything; you're raising a new problem. And I believe that the Judges will have to deliberate on this, and during the cross-examination I'm absolutely sure that Mr. Stringer will come back to this. So I'll stop here. We understand exactly what you said, but as far as conclusions are concerned, we'll see that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may facilitate things. I've held myself back, but it may be helpful to point out that the document P04494, which is at the basis of this, has been mistranslated into English. There are serious deficiencies, and this is the gist of my intervention. In the introductory sentence in the Croatian language, Blaskic says: "On the basis of Article 34, paragraph 2, of the Bylaw on the Armed Forces of the HVO HZ-HB," a consolidated version, "and pursuant to the authority of the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of HVO HZ-HB, number 396," et cetera, but in English the second leg of the second ground has been omitted. So the grounds are not just Article 34, paragraph 2, but also the legal grounds for adoption of this document was the authority or authorisation given by the commander-in-chief, and this is what General Praljak rightly pointed out. So unlike other commanders of operation zones, Mr. Blaskic had such authority, and this is an atypical. Furthermore, the order of things has been mixed up later in the document, and you do not have to know both languages to notice that this is a very shabby translation, translated by the Prosecution. We should not rely blindly on them. So that authorisation that Mr. Blaskic invokes, and that authorisation coming from the commander-in-chief, has been adduced as an exhibit as P00280. I believe had we noticed this at the very beginning, it would have shortened the discussion on this. I apologise, but I first had to check whether this was correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, Mr. Kovacic is saying that there's a translation problem. He's telling us that the text in B/C/S says that Colonel Blaskic appoints Vlado Cosic in application of Article 34, but according to the order of June 27, 1992, written by Mate Boban, and this is P0280. This text can be found there. Do you agree with this analysis of the document, because then Colonel Blaskic would be acting according to the powers that were given to him directly by Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. At page 21, line 12, replace "Mr. Bypass" with "Mr. Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is what I said, Your Honour. Because of the situation, Mr. Blaskic had such authority and he acted on it. If I may add on what you said. In wartime circumstances, there are two options or two possibilities. Either you face up to the facts and the reality, and adjust your structures to such reality in order not to use the war to reduce the level of evil, or, as you say, say, No, the structure will be as it is and I will stick to it, irrespective of whether it's functioning or not, for millions of reasons. I would like us to -- to give me a minute to be more precise in my explanation. So if at one place three houses are burning and three people are standing there, one can escape abroad and he's not guilty. The other waits for the fire brigade to arrive, but they're not arriving for some reasons. And the third one will jump and into the flames, he will put out the fire, although this is not his duty. He will rescue the people from those houses. And when he emerges, all singed and blackened, he will realise that he hasn't put out the fire in the third house. He may face the situation that, You are guilty because you have not saved all 5 three houses, and this is the essence of the war. Unfortunately, for many 6 reasons, the essential structures of organisations did not function. Either 7 people did not know how to do those things, they're incompetent, they lack 8 either courage or energy or funds or manpower, et cetera, et cetera. And 9 then you find yourself in a situation - let me finish this - to see that the 10 structure does not function, and you react. For instance, you remember the convoy in Citluk. So it was the civilians that stopped the convoy. For the convoy to go through, one should first talk to the civilians, and the person to do that should have been Mate Boban. So that was a political issue. But Mate Boban fails to appear for the talks, so Dr. Jadranko Prlic addresses the crowd. Dr. Jadranko Prlic fails because they're not listening to him. The next one up should be the head of the civilian police, because this is a crowd, it's got nothing to do with the military. Nevertheless, for one reason or another, the minister of the civilian police is just not around. Maybe he doesn't want to know about it or whatever. The whole situation is not working. Maybe the military police was in charge of making sure the convoy got through. I don't know. But I know that it wasn't the commander of the Main Staff who was in charge of making sure the convoy got through. Nevertheless, when they, for whatever reason, not necessarily a bad reason, fail, what I will do in a situation like that is get onto that convoy. I will run the risk of being shot by an angry parent, perhaps, but I will make sure the convoy gets through. In the process, I'm not changing anything structural about the fact that I am not technically the person in charge of that. I assume upon myself a duty that is outside any legal norms as to who should be doing what, exactly. So what happens is the following, Your Honours: The next problem crops up again. It's nothing to do with my job description. They realise that I took care of the previous one, so they come to speak to me again, the international community and whoever. Two options: You say, I refuse to do this, I don't care whether the convoy ever gets to Mostar or not, and people will go hungry; or you go back again and do something that you feel is your duty, although not necessarily under the law, because the commander of the Main Staff is in no way duty-bound to climb all over convoys and make sure they get through. But it was my duty as a human being, and that's what mattered in this war. When there was something that wasn't working, whoever is in a position to take over in a bid to save something, this doesn't mean -- it is not tantamount to relieving of his duty another person who should have done this in a line of his or her duty. Unfortunately, there were a great many situations like that, and I dealt with them myself, quite a number of those. I had to do someone else's job and assume upon myself someone else's duties, because for all sorts of reasons that other person was not willing or able to perform their task. These are the facts as we know them, and I will be telling you more about that later on. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. First of all, I would like to thank Mr. Kovacic for setting the English translation to right. Regardless of the English translation, I think everyone will agree that my reading of the Croatian document was accurate, the way I read it into the transcript. Therefore, everybody had a chance to hear what the phrasing was in the original text. We see here Mr. Blaskic invoking the authority of the supreme commander, and we know the document number as well. I have not lined up this document in my binder because I didn't believe that it would be of any relevance, but could we please call it up briefly in e-court. I think it would be useful for everyone here to see P00280 briefly, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the e-court copy is somewhat poor. Can you actually read the document? If not, we'll try and tackle the English, and then it will be interpreted to you by our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so you do. Fine. Mr. Praljak, I want to know about paragraph 2. Paragraph 2 reads: "The main commander appoints commanders of the HVO in Central Bosnia and is fully responsible for a complete articulation." All right. What I've been meaning to ask you is this: We've heard you say several times that the military police, with the exception of combat operations outside the HVO's military structure. Nevertheless, in paragraph 2 we see no mention of the military police. There is talk there of HVO commanders. I want to know: Is that in reference to the military police as well or is the military police simply not included in the substance of this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, the order is poorly written and it lacks the required technical background. What exactly is meant here by a complete articulation, good heaven knows, or the late Mate Boban. I have no idea who lined this document up for him. I really have no clue. It says what it says. I personally find it unclear. The commanders of this or that, a complete articulation. I don't think we would be getting very far if we looked further into that. Only the people who actually produced this could tell us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm not interested in this bit that says "a complete articulation." I'm interested in the bit about the commanders. You said a while ago that you knew Mr. Blaskic had the authority to appoint military police commanders based on this order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish. That was my understanding of your answer at the time. That is why I'm coming back to it. I'm looking at this document, I'm looking at paragraph 2, and I see no mention there of the military police. What about these HVO commanders? Does the category include HVO military police commanders or does it only include ordinary commanders in ordinary, regular units? That's what I want to know. Had you not said that any authority Blaskic had derived from this order by Mr. Boban, I would never have thought to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there is another order by Mate Boban, a later one, a much later one, issued sometime in the spring of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have an order the 27th of June, 1992, and it raises a few issues. We could understand that Colonel Blaskic has been appointed as chief of staff of the HVO, but there's a clarification that the person in charge is Ante Roso, but he is in charge of Central Bosnia, so he's wearing two hats. And as the person in charge of Central Bosnia, he's going to appoint the brigade commanders. Was that the situation? Was that how things had been split between the various people then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I don't know. Paragraph 1 of this order is clear. Paragraph 2 is unclear. I'm unable to comment on the meaning of this word here "articulation." Quite simply, you're asking me to interpret something that I find unclear. I did tell Ms. Tomic that I knew of Blaskic's authority in relation to the appointment of brigade commanders. He also had the power to use the military police in an operative way. Nevertheless, I said nothing about his power to appoint military police commanders. I didn't say it because I didn't know it. I did know, as a matter of fact, that he had the following two powers: A, to appoint HVO commanders, without necessarily seeking anyone's approval; that was the other thing, to use the military police in an operational sense. Your Honours, I only know what we see here. Mate Boban appoints the operation zone commanders and brigade commanders following proposals, nominations, you know, the usual procedure. We know all of the rest. What General Ante Roso was doing in this context is not something that I can tell you about. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, something brief about this document. A while ago, you told us you believe that there was a later authorisation written by Mr. Boban in relation to Mr. Blaskic. Can you look at this document, please, by Mate Boban. It's 396, it's right there in the header, and the date is the 27th of June, 1992. Can you now please go back to the other document authored by Mr. Blaskic, the appointment document. That is P00 -- P04494. I think we all have that one in front of us, but I think it invokes this specific document, 396, dated the 27th of June, 1992. Isn't it only logical -- hold on a minute. I'm about to ask you a question, because we're looking at this and we can all read, thank heavens. What I want to know is the following: Following this, Mr. Blaskic received another authorisation from Mr. Boban. Had that been the case, would he not have invoked the later order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Tomic, I said that with great precision. I said "perhaps." I didn't actually assert that there was another one. I said perhaps there was another one. Why did I say that? I actually talked to Mr. Boban about this in March 1993, following my return from Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you told us about that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there you go. That's why I said "perhaps." MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Can we now have P -- D04089. That's the next one up. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like to see whether I understood the last passage of this testimony. I seem to see that Tihomir Blaskic here appoints someone who normally he would not have the competence to appoint, and he refers to an order of Mate Boban which, in turn, is totally unclear and has a term "articulation" which at least the witness cannot make any sense of, and I will confess that I am in the same situation. Do I correctly wrap up what has been your testimony now, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite correct. I have no idea what "articulation" means. Again, I have no idea what the word "articulation" means or what Blaskic's interpretation of that expression was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I do apologise. In a technical sense, I don't think it really matters whether Praljak understands this or not, or anyone else, for that matter. The main thing is Blaskic understood Mate Boban's order. He invoked that order and he made the appointments. We cannot question whether Blaskic understood something or not just because Praljak didn't understand. Blaskic understood, and he made 150 appointments pursuant to this order. We've seen them all throughout this trial. Blaskic understands full well that Mate Boban, firstly paragraph 1, authorises him to exercise command over Central Bosnia and, paragraph 2, to appoint all the commanders there. I'm not going into anything else, but in a technical sense Blaskic does a great job understanding the order, and this applies throughout. We've seen at least 100 documents here. He stands by this order dated June. The fact that Mr. Praljak fails to understand this order, well, that is a problem related to Praljak's understanding, not Blaskic's. Blaskic did nothing against the law; quite the contrary. Boban vested him with certain authority, and Blaskic used that authority. Whether Praljak understands this or not is entirely beside the point. It is not my intention to offend anyone, but that is not material. Praljak doesn't understand. That doesn't necessarily mean that Blaskic didn't understand. We're not supposed to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Overlap between two speakers. We have not been able to interpret this, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I had to try to stop this because I think this is not correct. You are now pleading here and making explanations, and that should not be done. And, furthermore, what you are doing is a classical [Latin spoken]. You say that Mr. Tihomir Blaskic understood well because that's what he did, but the question, of course, is whether he did understand well and whether what he did here was, indeed, lawful. But that is something for the Chamber to decide, if necessary, and for the lawyers to argue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, if I may correct the transcript on page 30, line 15. It was a statement made by Petkovic, not by Pusic, as recorded in the transcript. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Counsel, Your Honours, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. General Praljak, there was a question I wanted to ask, and if I'd asked this question maybe the witness would -- the accused would not have stood up. You look at this document, this document is signed by Mate Boban, but also General Ante Roso, and you will notice that the document is coming from the Main Staff, so this document was drafted by General Roso and it has been signed by himself, and it was also signed by Mr. Boban, which means that Mr. Blaskic's authority had been determined in full agreement by Mr. Roso and Mr. Boban. And I understand the intervention of General Petkovic because this happened in 1992, and you know, General Praljak, that before you took office it was General Petkovic who was the commander of the HVO. And so you followed him in this position. When you took office on the 24th of July, were you aware that General Blaskic had this authority or not, and had General Petkovic failed to tell you that? This is what we are trying to ascertain here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew about the authorisations that Colonel Blaskic had in the Central Bosnia Operations Zone, and he acted according to and pursuant to the order as he understood it, and he issued orders, made decisions, appointed people, suspended people, in the way in which he understood the order giving him authorisation to do so. Nobody complained, nobody had any objections, so that functioned according to the military system in place. The fact that I don't understand what the word "articulation" means here is quite irrelevant, unimportant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would -- just to avoid any misunderstandings, I'm, of course, not in any way suggesting that Mr. Blaskic did something wrong, but I thought your point, Mr. Praljak, was that as he was completely isolated and had no contacts to his superiors, it was a sheer necessity for him to take the acts that were called for, including appointments which had to be made. Isn't that your point, the point you have tried to explain to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Judge Trechsel. The situation was such in Central Bosnia -- well, because Busovaca-Travnik, then an interruption, and then Kiseljak over here, or rather Busovaca-Kiseljak. Anyway, you cannot command and issue orders there unless you're there. It was only the people who were there that could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. I think that is a sensible proposition. Excuse me, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. You can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Judge Mindua had a question to ask. No? Okay, then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I'd just like to make one observation, and I'm referring to the remark made by Judge Trechsel when General Petkovic intervened and was on his feet. I agree that in procedural terms, that was perhaps improper, and I share Judge Trechsel's opinion there because it is difficult to say in what role General Petkovic intervened at that point in time. We all know that, and we're not challenging that. However, I do consider that it would be really negative if a message was to be sent out to the accused, or one of the accused or all of them, who for three and a half years have been sitting in this courtroom, to prevent them from intervening when they understand and see that the situation is quite unclear and that we're discussing something unnecessarily. And this is what General Petkovic felt, and he pinpointed the problem straight away. He saw where the problem lay. And so this specific reaction on General Petkovic's part, and these are my feelings and my sentiments, without a doubt helped us all to understand the situation because, if nothing else, he at least reminded us that he saw appointments of this kind, at least 150 of them, on the basis of that order. So please don't misunderstand me, but I do feel that we should not, a priori, reject any interventions which were not exaggerated. He did not stand up too frequently during this trial, and as far as I remember, they were always useful. They always contributed to the efficiency of the trial and to establishing the facts. So I should just like to prevail upon Judge Trechsel and ask him not to de-stimulate reactions of this kind for as long as they're not a problem, and they aren't a problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. I must say I agree with you, I agree with you. I did not want to blame Mr. Petkovic. I had the feeling that it went a bit long on, and that's why I then stopped him. But on principle, we are in full agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I sincerely apologise to all, and I'm going to be very sort of candid, because we're here and we've been discussing about these last two documents, and what I'm going to ask for is a clarification from the witness. And I do this with full acknowledgment that it is probably something that is more procedurally to be done on cross-examination, and so if counsel objects or if the Trial Chamber prefers that I wait, I will happily do that and come back to it. But since we're all here, this is a clarification that I would seek from the general. The general started when the general indicated there was an order from Mr. Boban that gave General Blaskic the authority to appoint brigade commanders, and I don't see that language in this document, and I know that the general's indicated he doesn't understand the language of the document. The document is also from a fairly early period, June 1992, when the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims really had not fully developed into the situation the general is describing of an encirclement and the rest. So the clarification I would seek, and I can -- I will withdraw the question and come back to it later, if that's what is decided, the question would be whether the general is aware whether any subsequent orders may have come from Mr. Boban to General Blaskic, defining his authority, as the situation between the Croats and the Muslims developed throughout 1993. So, again, I'll accept whatever treatment the parties and the Trial Chamber wish to give to my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stringer. I do not see, from a personal point of view, any objection for you to ask a clarification immediately, because we will gain time. And I would like to thank General Petkovic to have taken the floor, even if, according to the Rules and Regulations, it is not really provided for. But when you look at the normative text, they can say anything and everything, but in fact nothing prevents the accused from taking the floor and to say what he has to say. The only issue at stake is to know what the Judges will do with the probative value and that will have to be attributed to this sort of event where an accused is taking the floor. And I agree with counsel as well that we should not stop an accused from wanting to contribute and to make things clearer by stopping him from taking the floor. As you know, I would like everyone to be present in this courtroom, and very often when I have the feeling that accused do not understand or have the feeling that Judges are not listening to what they're saying, I do not feel comfortable, because this is not the concept of justice that I share. I feel that everyone should be free to express themselves, and of course within the framework of the normative texts that are upon us. But the normative texts allow us to do quite a lot of things. So it has happened in the past that Mr. Prlic took the floor to clarify certain things, as well as Mr. Stojic, and I think it was always beneficial to the proceedings. We see that there is an issue which has been also raised by Mr. Stringer, namely, it's an order dating back to June 1992, and the question is whether Central Bosnia, as the general was saying, was encircled. And we understand very well what the situation is, so Mr. Stringer is making us understand that there might be a real issue at stake here, and waiting until the cross-examination to get a clarification could also be detrimental to the proceedings. So, Mr. Praljak, you have heard what everyone has said, and I also had the same line of thought as Mr. Stringer. We were wondering whether, in June 1992, Central Bosnia was encircled in such a way that Boban had only this solution. But you didn't tell us this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, in June, Central Bosnia was not under an encirclement to the extent that you couldn't reach it. I said this in very precise terms, and let me repeat it for the benefit of the Prosecution. I was telling you what I know about, and it is this, and you have some documents to bear that out, and you are going to ask me about them, I assume. In March 1993, I was in Central Bosnia after an agreement had been signed to calm the situation down and so on and so forth, and at the time Mr. Blaskic asked me to convey to Boban, Petkovic, and so on that according to his forecasts, the BH Army was getting ready to attack the HVO. Now, it was a very difficult situation. It was difficult to move along the roads. I was in a car with an escort, and they said, If we come across a BH Army check-point, for example, Paraga, one of Paraga's units, the car behind me had to stop 50 metres away from me, and if they saw me reaching for my rifle, that they should start shooting straight away because it was very easy to be killed by some murderers, some killers. And upon my return, I asked Mate Boban -- on the way back, I asked Mate Boban to enable Tihomir Blaskic, because communications were down, in actual fact, to enable him, in operational terms, to deploy, without having to have us down the chain of command and ask the military police, to deploy for military purposes the military police. Mate Boban told me that it had all been dealt with, that it was all settled. So it was on the basis of that piece of information that I'm able to tell you what I'm saying here and now. So that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we understand correctly, because you could have said that earlier on, the text that we have before us is a mere consequence of a discussion you had with Mate Boban, you had realised the ABiH was going to launch an attack, and therefore you had to give Mr. Blaskic the full authority to react to any attack. And the document that we have before us has to be understood in this context; namely, the request that you had put to Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I made the request in March 1993. I didn't even know that this document existed, but obviously Mate Boban said it's all been settled. Well, he probably thought that it had already been issued or whatever. So there's this difference in time, from the time I made my request to Tihomir Blaskic and Mate Boban's reply that it had been dealt with or would be settled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But how is it that in June 1992, Mate Boban is giving his -- is vesting Blaskic with the power to appoint people? Is there a political reason for this? If it's not because Central Bosnia is encircled, what's the reason behind all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you want my interpretation of events. I don't know what the reason could have been, but I can tell you what I think the reason was or might have been. So I ask the interpreters to use the correct tenses there and say what I'm saying. The HVO is being created, established, so in that area, and there was major fighting going on with the Serbs, so probably they didn't have time to provide information, CVs, go into various checks, verifications and so on, because the army was growing at such a great rate because of the battles in Jajce, in Vlasic, and so on and so forth. Mate Boban most probably, and that is my opinion, most probably says, Go ahead, appoint commanders over there according to your selection, your choice. So what would it mean if somebody were to send him in a proposal for an appointment or send in a nomination when that person knew nothing about the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For what it's worth, it's an explanation. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] We're coming up to the break, but I have one more document. May I go ahead with that, related Mr. Blaskic and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Show your document and then we'll have the break. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Document 5D04089. It's the next document in the set, and this document is a commendation signed by Tihomir Blaskic. 5D04089 is the document number. As I was saying, it's signed by Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document is dated the 18th of April, 1993. That means before your arrival, before your arrival there as commander of the HVO, and this is a document in which Mr. Blaskic is issuing commendations to the members of the 4th Military Police Battalion and their commander for the valour and courage they showed in carrying out their assignments. Do you know about this, and is it in conformity with the authority that Colonel Blaskic had and the kind of authority that we've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A, let me say that I don't know of this document and, B, the authority and powers of -- well, we have two things here; first of all, Blaskic's authority to deploy the 4th Military Police Battalion in the first place for military purposes. And the third point, point C, is his right to commend somebody for having taken part in a battle and for fighting bravely and well. So there are three points there. He could, of course, commend individuals. I could commend individuals, too. I could commend any military police unit while it was taking part in the military operations, and I happened to notice that they were good guys. I could do that, but it just so happened that I did not. But this is quite a usual commendation. There's nothing contentious there. He considered that they merited commendation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, April 18 is two days after Ahmici. I don't know whether the 4th Battalion was involved in Ahmici, I don't have the judgement at hand, but I did note that it was two days after Ahmici. Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now that you've told me about that, I see that it is, indeed, two days after Ahmici. I don't know if the 4th Battalion took part, I do not know that, but I interpreted and was responding to the questions asked by Ms. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Let me tell the counsel, Mr. Coric's counsel, that she's already used one hour and seventeen minutes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Before I continue my examination, I would like to ask everybody in the courtroom, and I believe that this is the best interests of the Defence of Mr. Coric, as follows: There is a precedent by Mr. Karnavas. This is reasonable, and the Prosecution, I believe, did the same. I'm trying, in my cross-examination, just as the Prosecution has done, trying to put forward the case for Mr. Coric, I'm going to -- I'm trying to proceed slowly and bring the witness, step by step, to the point I'm trying to make. What I'd like to ask is as follows: After each issue that I'm going to finish, and they're not going to be long, to stop and break and give the opportunity to everybody in the courtroom to ask questions, object, because if we proceed in this way I'm afraid that even though I may exhaust the list of my questions, they may be lost and my point would be lost. So every time I think I've accomplished what I tried to accomplish, I'm going to say, I'm done with this subject, does anybody else have any questions? And I would be very grateful if we could proceed this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will try, but you must understand us, when we have a document on the screen, sometimes there are follow-up questions regarding the document. Of course, we don't know what you intend to do. Of course, we have the binders. So if I notice that in the document there is an answer, I don't put the question. We'll try to do what you've asked us to do. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Following up on the issue that we discussed before the break, I'm going to work on two documents in succession, and it will be easy for you to revisit them after I'm done with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please, Mr. Praljak, let's take a look at document 5D04394, in the same binder, the following document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It purports to be your document, dated 31st of July, 1993, addressed to the Main Staff of the HVO Mostar, to the Military Police Administration at Mostar, attention of Mr. Valentin Coric and Mr. Perica Turajlija. It is entitled "Instructions for the VP Administration" or "Military Police Administration," and it states as follows: "The order that you issued on 29 July 1993, number ...," I'm not going to read it out, "... on the suspension of the platoon commander of military police, Perica Turajlija, and his relief of duty will not be implemented. "Perica Turajlija's military police platoon is under my operational command and is carrying out all its assigned tasks. "Relief of duty will be carried out by you only after the conduct of an investigation with the presentation of solid evidence." Mr. Praljak, could you please tell us whether you remember this incident and whether I've read out what it really states in the document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written in this document is true. I authored it, I signed it, and I dispatched it. I can provide you with an explanation now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you what I'm interested in. At this point, I'm not interested in whether you were right or Mr. Coric was right, who was trying to relieve Mr. Turajlija of his duty. What I'm interested in is whether you thought that you had the right, in circumstances where you did not see that there was evidence for somebody breaching disciplinary procedures and the commander is under your operational command, that he could not be relieved of his duty, although Mr. Coric wanted to do so. This is what I'm after.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under circumstances obtaining, I believe that this was so for the simple reason is that what I'm stating in this document is that Mr. Coric was not doing the job properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you deemed that Mr. Coric was not doing his job properly. Right. Okay. I'm not challenging or wanting to discuss who did what and whether they did their job properly. My intention is that you, when you thought it was right, you had the right to do so. And you answered my question, and let's proceed to another question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I…

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, please. Your interpretation of law follows from the state of facts based on which I take that right. This is not scholastics, but war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, please don't be cross. You've answered my question, and I'm following with another document, P03934. Let's take a look at it. This document was dated later, dated the 4th of August, 1993, concerning the relief of units of duty. It is addressed to Gornji Vakuf units. This is another of your documents, and among the addressees you see Military Police Turajlija as one of the addressees at the end of list. What I'd like to ask you about this document is: Is it apparent from this document, and was this really so, that Mr. Turajlija continued performing his duties under your operational command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one question in relation to that. Mr. Praljak, do you know that as per establishment of the military police of the HVO, there was no unit entitled "Military Police Turajlija"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a military police platoon under the command of Turajlija, and this is why I labelled it so, because the Commander Andabak, up to that point, had fled from his position for four times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already mentioned that person.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that. On the 1st, so when I regained the positions in Vakuf, at a meeting Mr. Prlic attended, as well as I did, and after almost panic reigned after the fall of Vakuf, which I regained with my lads, I reacted very strongly, seeing Andabak there, and said to Coric, That person will have to face court-martial for leaving his positions four times, as far as I knew, about four times him leaving his positions, and nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, Mr. Andabak will be another issue. We are going to deal with it. I would like to tell Their Honours that I am finished with those two documents, and now I give the opportunity to everybody to ask about those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in the last document on the screen, I was looking at the recipient list. I see there's "HV Hrvatinic Brigade, brigade Hrvatinic." What is it exactly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the Brigade Hrvoje Vukcic-Hrvatinic. There was some confusion about this brigade being Croatian. These are remnants of a brigade from Jajce, residual manpower of that brigade who did not leave the territory of Bosnia- Herzegovina. It was called "brigade," but in terms of its strength, it could not meet the requirements of a company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question. This is August 4th, almost two weeks after you took command. I see the number on this document. At "1147," does this mean that in 15 days, you signed 1147 documents or did you just take over the numbers after Mr. Petkovic's command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Numbers were taken over. No, maybe I wrote 10, 15 orders in that time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you recollect, how many documents did you sign a day, on average?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, it's very difficult for me to say. One, two documents, not more. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let's take a look at three documents in a row, and this will bring to a close my cross-examination concerning disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, answering my learned friend Alaburic's question and Judge Trechsel's questions, recorded on page 42483 of the transcript, you said that military disciplinary courts were never established, that you were not in charge of their establishment, and that Mate Boban did not establish them either, presuming, therefore, that it was incumbent upon Mate Boban to do so, looking up -- at the model of the Republic of Croatia. And you stated that on several occasions on the same page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For what I know, military disciplinary courts did not function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at document P05279. This is a document that's been repeatedly shown to you during examination-in-chief and examination of the Presiding Judge. This is your order on serving of disciplinary detention prison sentences imposed by the commander. You addressed this order, this document, to all operation zones and directly subordinated units of the Main Staff, and presidents of military disciplinary courts of first and second instance. Mr. Praljak, when taking into account, after seeing this document, the fact that you said that there were no military disciplinary courts, could you please explain now that you're issuing an order to military disciplinary courts if they did not exist; alternatively, that you knew that they did not exist? I don't understand that, and I'm not helped by the document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not clear, based on this document. I have to say that I would draft such documents, and most frequently General Matic would write them down. I would give him the gist of the order, and the deputy commander of the Main Staff, General Matic, who signed many of those orders. As a general in the JNA, he was trained to draft such orders. I did sign this document, I drafted it. It is true that it states that there were military disciplinary courts, but I maintain, irrespective of my signature here, when I asked commanders of companies to mete out disciplinary sanctions, they did so, but there was no procedure in terms of three officers sitting on a bench and hearing evidence. Nothing of the sort happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I presume that you read this document before you signed it. This order, I mean. And I'm interested in this: Did you ask General Matic why military disciplinary courts have been mentioned here if they did not exist?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree there is a discrepancy between what is written here and what the reality was, but on the 22nd of September, when I had some ten minutes for the business of Main Staff, because this is the time of the Neretva-93 offensive, I could just scan the document, see "Dretelj Prison," some key words, and then sign it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the second document, P2 -- 002022, P00 -- 5D, correction, 5D02022. This is a document signed by Mr. Ante Govorusic. He's deputy commander of the Herzegovina operation zone, and it's addressed to all commands of Operation Zone of Western Herzegovina. From the heading, we can see pursuant to an order of the Main Staff, and the content of the order, we see that it refers to your earlier order that we discussed a minute ago, in terms of meting out disciplinary sanctions. The among the addressees, we can see that there are brigades, 6th Military Police Battalion, 2nd Light Assault Battalion of Military Police, and Lateral Battalion, Prozor, et cetera. Tell us, Mr. Praljak, did you know whether this document was distributed down the chain of command to operations zone and their subordinate units within the area of responsibility of those zones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is supposed to be so, as per regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at the last document concerning this, P07361. This is a document dating after the time while you were in charge. At the time of this document, Ante Roso was chief of the Main Staff. It's dated 28th December 1993. It is addressed to all military districts. And in this document, Mr. Roso says as follows: "Pursuant to the regulations of Article 52, paragraph 2, of the Rules of Procedure on Military Discipline, and regarding the formation of a court of military discipline, I hereby issue an order."
