Item 1: "To establish a court of military discipline for the military district." Item 2: "The court of military discipline shall sit with a chamber of three judges." And then it follows to list the president and the members of the chamber. In item 3, what is discussed is the appointment of the registrar, and in item 4 it is said military district commanders are going to be responsible for the execution of this order, and they are duty-bound to submit a written report on this by the 3rd of January, 1994. Mr. Praljak, I'm not going to ask you whether you've seen this document because it was generated after you left your duty, but it is based, as we can see, on the Rules of Procedure of Military Discipline, and my question is as follows: Can you explain to us how it is that Mr. Roso thinks that it was incumbent upon him, as chief of the Main Staff, to issue such an order on the establishment of courts of military discipline, and you, yourself, stated that you did not see it as incumbent upon you to do so and that they did not exist?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still think that I don't know exactly. Nevertheless, if you look at the Croatian Army model, my conviction remained that the courts of military discipline had to be set up by the army's supreme commander. It is quite obvious that the chief of the Main Staff, who followed in my steps, in my footsteps, Ante Roso, thought differently. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm done on the subject of discipline and am about to move on to a different topic. I'm not sure if anyone has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] My next subject is criminal proceedings. There are three documents in your binder. Four, as a matter of fact. I misspoke. Four documents. First of all, could we please have 4D01317 pulled up in e-court, a document conveniently put together by the Petkovic Defence, containing a number of relevant provisions from the Decree on the Military District Courts and the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, Maitre Alaburic asked you about the authorities of a commander when criminal proceedings are in progress. Essentially, you responded that the duties of a commander are only in reference to situations in which the perpetrator isn't identified, when a perpetrator was caught "in flagrante" while committing an act, caught red-handed, as it were. Whenever the perpetrator remained unidentified, this ceases to be the job of the commander. Rather, it was the security bodies in the armed forces that would have been in charge of situations like these.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to my learned friend. I think this is an inaccurate summary of witness testimony. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I don't think this is inaccurate, and Mr. Praljak is perfectly free to correct me if I'm wrong and whether the whole thing is inaccurate. But during the next break, I can bring you the transcript pages that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can clarify, if you'd like me to. At no point in my cross-examination did I say anything about a perpetrator being caught "in flagrante." I was only talking about the responsibility to prevent any perpetrators from hiding or escaping. The only logical conclusion would be that the perpetrator was in the commander's hands, but there was nothing being said about a perpetrator being caught "in flagrante" or during the commission of a criminal offence. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I will correct myself, then, and I will say let's leave all of this aside, although I do believe that Mr. Praljak used the term "in flagrante."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was later on. It wasn't during Ms. Alaburic's cross-examination. It was later on I said, in addition to something else, that this was in reference to a fact that you lawyers would tend to call "in flagrante." That's precisely what I said, what you lawyers would call that. When a brigade commander comes across -- the commander of a company or a battalion, comes across something like this, he is duty-bound to take steps pursuant to this paragraph. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I was about to say. He needs to know who the perpetrator is. If that is not the case, then it's down to the security organs within the armed forces to track down the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just those from the armed forces, but also the civilian police, the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, any kind of police whatsoever, plus the SIS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I was driving at. I was just taking a shortcut in order to avoid wasting more time. Nevertheless, let us go to paragraph 25 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. On another topic, let's move to a private session just for a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic was showing you Article 25, which is on the next page of this document 4D, Article 25 of the Decree on the District Military Courts. The Article states, as you were shown by Ms. Alaburic -- the last part of the Article states that according to this decree, it would be the authorised officials of the security organ of the armed forces that would be in charge of these activities. You do remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I would like to move on to Article 151 on that same page to see what the Law on Criminal Procedure says as far as it defines the job of the Ministry of the Interior and its various bodies. Let's look at Article 151. It reads: "If there are grounds to suspect that a criminal act that is prosecuted ex officio has been committed, the law enforcement agencies must take all the steps necessary to locate the perpetrator of the criminal act, to prevent the perpetrator or accomplice from hiding or fleeing, to discover and secure any criminal evidence or, indeed, items which might be used in evidence, and to gather any information which might be of use to an effective conduct of criminal proceedings." Mr. Praljak, I will now ask you a hypothetical question in relation to the Article that we just read. If it is true that all these jobs that I have just specified, in terms of uncovering a crime and any further steps that are taken following the commission of a crime, is something that would have been incumbent upon the security organs of the armed forces, then it is not necessary to pass any other regulations, with the exception of Article 25, which is the one that we read a while ago, stating that any jobs that, under the Law on Criminal Procedure, are done by bodies of the Ministry of the Interior, would be done, as far as the military disciplinary courts were concerned, by the security organs of the armed forces, themselves; am I right in stating that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to object to this question and this whole line of questioning. This material was prepared in order to obtain a parallel view of the Law on Criminal Procedure, on the one hand, and the law passed by the HZ-HB. Why? If I may invoke Mr. Buntic's testimony. I'm trying to simplify, but that is the general message. When a law talks -- for example, a military court, the regular law that existed before the war, then the HZ-HB, in its regulations, normally specified the military court in question, because the old military court from the pre-war law is no longer around. Yugoslavia broke up; we all know that. Nevertheless, why am I saying all of this? This requires a legal analysis. Mr. Buntic was in a position to testify about that. We can have another expert witness, or perhaps we can use the presence of a witness that might be in possession of relevant knowledge. Nevertheless, Mr. Praljak is certainly not that witness. How this was resolved under the Law on Criminal Procedure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and how a certain legal institute was adopted to form part of the HZ-HB regulations in order for the existing laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be used, merely those elements and those institutes where something was being adapted, which military court, which authorised official, and so on and so forth. Mr. Praljak is certainly not the person to tell us about that. He's simply not qualified for that. Ms. Alaburic's questions were of a different nature. She said, How do you understand this, or, Are you the person, but we cannot have a comparison of this kind. Ms. Alaburic made this comparison just for us lawyers to understand what she was talking about, or at least that was my reading of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you had your counsel stating that given the legal complexity of the questions, he feels that he has to raise an objection. As far as you are concerned, do you feel in a position to answer or is it really beyond your knowledge, and did you know that if there were a prosecutor, a president, and judges at tribunals, but we should not go further into details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not wish to go beyond that. Before the war, during the war and after the war, I knew exactly: A, what would have constituted the criminal responsibility of a citizen; B, what violations of the Law of War were, all of them; and, C, I knew exactly what military commanders were to do about this; D, take disciplinary procedure, be it prepare a report protecting someone whom they may have found, bringing someone in, or if they weren't up to it, leaving all of this to the military prosecutor or to a civilian, a military service, an investigation of an unknown perpetrator, for example. But that's where I left it. My job was to teach any and all commanders I came across what the Rules of War were, the rules of engagement, and what they were to do whenever they came across violations of that law. Bring them in, if you can; if not, just report them whenever you learn something, and then leave it to all the other institutions that were in charge of just that. Zoran Buntic was there for it. There were other people who were dealing with that. I'm reluctant to make any comparisons. Was it down to a civilian body? Who was the perpetrator? A soldier who had left his position along the front-line and simply gone home, I really can't say. This is outside the scope of what I can talk about or address with any degree of precision whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel, questions can be of a complex nature. Counsel Kovacic raised an objection, and General Praljak said that his knowledge was limited to main principles, so he does not wish for you to go into details because it could mislead the Chamber or himself. So please ask very simple questions, and please do not go too much into legal details. I will give you an example of what not to do; namely, who has authority or jurisdiction if a crime is committed by a soldier on a civilian or by a soldier on another soldier, what does the civil police, what does the military police? This would go beyond his area of competence, so please ask very simple questions. Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will do my best to simplify, as much as I can, in asking my questions. Nevertheless, I just read an article of the law, which is precisely the same thing that Ms. Alaburic did. At the time, Mr. Praljak did not declare himself to be incompetent, but I'll try to ask simpler questions in order to avoid this sort of situation. Now I will just simply read the articles out and I will say, Did you know about this? I will not compare anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic, please don't misinterpret my words. I said I know what the duty of a commander is when he realises or is aware of the fact that during his operation or after his operation, a crime is committed. This perfectly clear. He must secure the area and secure any evidence that is there. Whenever able to track down a perpetrator, he must do just that, isolate the perpetrator and then throw him in jail. He must then leave it to all the other institutions to prosecute, to sentence, to convict, and all of that. The part that I'm familiar with, I am perfectly familiar with. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'll be asking you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another objection, in that case. We know what the purpose is and what should be covered by cross-examination. Since my learned friend has just made this very specific, this cross-examination is about those subjects and theories that were the subject of another cross-examination, that of the Petkovic Defence. This is not a cross-examination. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I do not agree with my learned friend Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, just a minute, please. I do agree -- I do believe that my learned friend should be asking questions about subjects that were raised in-chief, or link her own questions to issues raised during the chief, such as the Chamber's questions, but this is a second cross and it's simply unrelated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since Mr. Kovacic raises an objection that I wanted to make, and actually he refers to my cross-examination, but I'll refrain from reacting, I would like to raise an objection of principle with respect to the Coric cross-examination of this witness because it is cross-examination of General Petkovic's cross-examination. We would like to -- well, we would like the Trial Chamber to rule whether this is the kind of cross-examination that is allowed. And this cross-examination on the cross-examination of another Defence team is allowed in this court, if that is what the ruling is, then I would like to ask for additional time for my own kind of redirect to this cross-examination of a cross-examination. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to respond? General Praljak, I will respond to that. I am very astonished that Mr. Kovacic is objecting and saying that my cross-examination was not linked to the examination-in-chief, and he failed to object to Ms. Alaburic, because if my cross-examination was not linked to the examination-in-chief, but was linked to the cross-examination of Ms. Alaburic, then it would follow that it was Ms. Alaburic which went beyond the scope of cross-examination. That's my first point. My second point is this: With respect to the authority and what the authority and powers of the military police was, and whose job it was to find the perpetrators of a crime, and whose job it was to table criminal reports, is something that General Praljak talked about in response to questions raised during the examination-in-chief and during Judge Antonetti's questioning, so during my cross-examination, I do have the right to put to him the provisions and rules for him to explain who was authorised to do what. Now, Mr. Praljak can say that he didn't know about these rules and regulations or that it says something else there, but as regards Ms. Alaburic's direct and redirect, then I'd like to raise the question of whether, in fact, Ms. Alaburic conducted an examination-in-chief and then I am conducting a cross-examination, or what. I don't know what we're talking about here. All I know is that I referred to Ms. Alaburic because she was the last person to ask that question, and Mr. Praljak gave the same answers to Judge Antonetti as he did during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down for the benefit of one and all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I be allowed to contribute to this discussion and present General Petkovic's position in just one sentence? My objection did not relate to the topics discussed, because during the examination-in-chief it is true that a whole series of subjects were broached, so we cannot say with any certainty about any subject, that it was not covered in one way or another in the examination-in-chief. My objection exclusively referred to my learned colleague referring to my questions and responses given to my questions, and the summarisation of something that was represented as being the cross-examination of General Petkovic of this witness. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] May I respond to Ms. Alaburic first, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait. General Praljak is fretting about, and so I will give him the floor, and then you can take the floor. So what did you want to say, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to say, Your Honours, regardless of what your ruling is going to be, that I am ready to answer any question put to me by anybody. I can say I know about that, I don't know about that. I can tell them what my knowledge was, why something was done at a given point in time. So I'm ready to do that. But all I'm asking is that I be allowed to finish my answers and give a complete answer. If I don't know about something, then I state that loud and clear, I say, I don't know. But if I do know something, then I would like to be allowed to answer. So you can all ask any questions you wish to ask, regardless of whether the issues were raised during the examination-in-chief or whenever. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all I wanted to say was this: I didn't know that it would lead to such a heated debate and be reduced to formal terms, that I'm referring to what Ms. Alaburic said during the cross-examination, particularly because she addressed the Stojic Defence and would say, The Stojic Defence put to you such and such. So I didn't think there were any restrictions for me to go on and ask and refer to what Ms. Alaburic had asked during her cross-examination. But as I say, in future I'm not going to do it that way, I'm not going to say, As Ms. Alaburic said. I'm going to present my case with the essential points, without linking it to the Petkovic Defence, but I will just refer to what was stated in the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, what is the position of the Prosecution on the fact that an accused can cross-examine another accused during this phase, the Defence case, for the Defence case? Is it possible, is it not possible; what is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think that my first observation would be that the witness, having been testifying now, I think, for nine weeks, there isn't really anything that I can think of that is outside the scope of what has been raised before, and so I think, as the general himself as indicated, really, his own intention -- and I think that procedurally we're in a place that really everything is within the scope of something that's been raised before by one team or another or by the Trial Chamber, itself, in its own questioning. In terms of allocations among the Defence, as the Trial Chamber knows, the Prosecution is usually hesitant to get too involved in that. It's essentially a trial management issue. I think that I would agree with something. I think that it may have been Judge Trechsel or another member of the Bench said it at one time earlier, which is that -- I think it was during the cross-examination by my learned friend Ms. Alaburic. There was an observation whether General Petkovic's interests were aligned with those of General Praljak on an issue, and I think that that is a point that's worth bearing in mind, that as between all of the Defence teams there are issues in which some of them actually may be in alignment, whereas obviously there are going to be other issues where their interests are not in alignment and where there are going to be issues which give rise to what, in our view, is genuine cross-examination, and that's what's happening here. So I guess the Trial Chamber, I think, is clearly seeing that. If this is now cross-examination in response to an issue that was raised by Ms. Alaburic in what might be more correctly thought of as a friendly examination, if I may put it that way, and this is a phrase that the Prosecution has used previously, then if it's friendly, then maybe it's more in the field of direct, and if so there may be a situation where the Trial Chamber might want to allow another Defence team to come back with follow-up questions in the way that another team might want to follow up on questions that come from the Trial Chamber. So -- but, again, this is obviously primarily a trial management issue, and so beyond that I don't think the Prosecution has a position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. I seem to recall that we had this kind of discussion a number of times here. From both sides, there have been objections, but we have always pointed out to the Rules of Procedure, which say that in cross-examination, any party may take up a point which is important for that party's case. And I think we have always been rather liberal in this respect, and I would say that in this case, too, there's no reason, really, to stop Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic in continuing in the line that she has started. I wonder whether my colleagues agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to say, Mr. President, that if there's going to be a ruling on this, we certainly would like to be heard, and I think the rest of the Defence teams should be heard on this matter, since the Prosecution has stated its position. So that's all I wanted to say at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we are really wasting time, while we have an accused who is only asking one thing, is to answer questions that he's in a position to answer, so this is really an obvious matter. But there's something that I have really not understood. I would like to know why Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic would be in conflict or in opposition or would have any dissenting opinion on one point or another. I haven't had this feeling until now, but maybe counsels are in conflict between themselves. But I don't have the feeling that, between the two accused, that there is a conflict. As to trying to identify the topic, Ms. Tomic could have said, Well, by answering the question from Ms. Alaburic, you said this, that, and that on page such and such. So we have to be in a position to frame the issue very carefully. As for your answer, the answer you said, that it is not in agreement with Article 148 or 127, I don't know. I will show you the article, what do you think? This is the way you could have phrased the question, because maybe that from the outset Mr. Praljak is not in a position with Mr. Petkovic. Maybe he did not answer a question properly because he made a mistake. But it seems that it immediately triggers objections. Counsel Karnavas stands up and says everyone should be able to have a position, whereas, in fact, in the judgement it will never be touched upon because we have spent quite a lot of time on this and it will not be relevant. So what I would like to know for my own understanding, Ms. Tomic, is: What is the problem here, what is the issue here? Could you please tell me what was the issue that you wanted to bring to light here? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, had I managed to go from Article 151 to Article 27 of the Decree on District Military Courts, then we would have seen what the problem was, but I haven't reached that point yet. So might I be allowed to do that. I'm not going to ask for any further interpretations or what follows from what, but I'm going to ask about what is quite obvious and whether General Praljak knew about it or not, so in the next questions five minutes you are going to understand. It's going to be made clear what I'm actually getting at, am talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber rejects the objection of Mr. Kovacic. We did not feel that everyone should be consulted, and we are asking Mr. Coric's counsel to carry on with the questions. But we ask her not to ask questions of a too-legal nature because it is obvious that his limited legal skills will not allow him to answer certain questions if they were put in that way. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since we've been having this debate for quite some time now, I'd like to remind the Court of what it says in Article 151 because it's important. This Article regulates the affairs of the organs of the interior, and it says that they are duty-bound to take all necessary steps to find the perpetrator, to prevent him from absconding or going into hiding, and to uncover and secure the traces and evidence, any objects that can be used in evidence, and to gather all other necessary information. So that was from the code governing criminal proceed. Now I'd like us to go back to the first page of this document, where we will find Article 27 of the decree or provision governing military district courts, and it says there, in para 1, the commander of a military police unit or military institution must take all necessary measures to prevent the perpetrator of a crime under official prosecution from going into hiding or from escaping, and they must attempt to preserve all the traces of the crime and all other objects that may serve as evidence. They must also gather all information relevant to the criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, when we look at Article 151 that I read out a moment ago of the Law on Criminal Procedure, and Article 27, para 1, of the Military District Courts, and if you compare the two, would you agree with me when I say, and did you know about it, that the commander, under the provision governing military district courts, has the duty of seeing to all those affairs and duties which are listed under Article 151 of the Code on Criminal Procedure, which by that Article, it was the organs of internal affairs that were duty-bound to conduct those duties, except for uncovering the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and that is, in fact, the essential point, to find the perpetrator. That is at the crux of the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to that. I'd just like to say that on page 65 of the record, of the transcript, on line 13 it says that in paragraph -- it says that the commander of the military police [as interpreted], well, where it says "military police unit," I said "the commander of a military unit."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there, and I'd like to add that we're dealing with the commander of a military unit and within the remits of a military unit, who's going to secure the site and who's going to apprehend a perpetrator in Mostar, Rama, whatever municipality?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll come to that. We're not at odds, you and me. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I think that you understood a difficult question that was put to you by counsel, but in order for me to understand your answer, I have a few questions. Counsel made a comparison, and she talked about Article 151, which -- as states that the investigating services have the duty to look for perpetrators of crimes and to look for suspects, so of course we think of the civil police, the military police, the investigating magistrates or judges, the military prosecutor, as well as the investigating judges. And there is this text from Article 27, which says that it's the brigade commander who has then to fulfill a number of tasks immediately to make sure that the suspected perpetrator absconds and to make sure that the scene of the crime is preserved by taking all necessary measures. So the counsel is asking you whether Article 27 doesn't mean that the brigade commander has a responsibility which he didn't used to have, and you answered by "yes." Did you understand that exactly, which means that the brigade commander, as a result of this normative text, must, as soon as he's been made aware of a crime, give orders to the military police and actually also to soldiers to preserve the scene of the crime and to arrest the perpetrators if they are caught in the act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, and I see nothing -- no discrepancies there. You have your area of responsibility, the front-line, an action or operation. Now, if a commander -- well, if the military police learns about it, then it's their duty. If the commander learns about it, then it's his duty, but it is not his duty to uncover the perpetrator of a crime. He has no possibility of doing that, and that's the essential difference. If I catch somebody who has committed some act, then I grab him by the neck and I wait for the others to come and get him. It's very simple. I don't see why we are having all this discussion. If somebody in this courtroom commits any untoward act, I'm the strongest one here in the courtroom, I would apprehend him and then hand him over to the guards, and then all the other institutions do that. That is my civic duty. I did this as a civilian before the war. For example, I had occasion to run faster than somebody who was involved in a traffic accident and caused a traffic accident, and I apprehended him. Here it's the commander's duty, if he knows about it, if he knows an act has been committed and he can do something about it, but that is 0.1 per cent or 0.01 per cent of the cases. Everything else happens in the rear at night, clandestinely, and so on and so forth, and a commander cannot investigate such matters. He can only learn of them by chance. And if he happens to learn of them by chance, once again it is his duty to convey that information to the investigative organs. And there you have it. For instance, in Ljubuski people get drunk at a cafe, having returned from a 30-day stint at the front-line. Their offences are exchanged, tempers rise. Somebody takes out a gun and shoots another person. And if a commander is there, then he would apprehend the perpetrator, and this is the "in flagrante" situation. That's clear. There have been such cases, and all perpetrators were apprehended. But the other cases which this court deals with were, unfortunately, furtively perpetrated, as criminals are inclined to do, and I'm talking about violations of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we have Article 27 on the screen, let's take a look at paragraph 2, which reads: "All of the information referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article, commander of a military unit or military institution is duty-bound to deliver such information to the district military prosecutor or their immediate superior officer." Mr. Praljak, does it follow from this, and whether you knew about this, that a military commander was duty-bound to inform the military prosecutor on what he had done and that the military prosecutors take over?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reading further, we are discussing here information and not a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the extent of my understanding. There can't be talk of any criminal report. He reports, he delivers the information, and then criminal reports follow an investigation, and everything else will be done according to the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the same page, we have Article 148 which has a heading "Criminal Report." Let's take a look at the bolt, paragraph 3, which reads: "In launching an allegation, government agencies and organisations of associated labour, and other self-management organisations and communities, shall present evidence known to them and shall take steps to preserve traces of a criminal offence, objects upon which or with which the criminal act was committed, and other evidence." Do you agree with me, and whether you knew about that, that what follows from this is that everybody was duty-bound to file criminal reports, not only commanders, but all organisations of associated labour -- there is this term "socialist," but we know what we're talking about. All bodies and organisations were duty-bound to file criminal reports, furnish documents or evidence corroborating their report? I'm trying to simplify things here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Madam Tomic. One thing is to inform and quite another thing is to file a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I concur, I concur. This is why I've shown you those two articles. Now let us take a look at document 4D01105, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I listened to what you said, but you have already answered my question. I don't really see what is the added value of the questions put to you today, but Defence can do what it wants. But let me come back to this. You already told us when answering my questions. You told me that for you, crimes were usually done at night or on the field, but after the military operation. As far as night is concerned, we know that there were cases, like in Prozor, where people would come at night to take the prisoners. We're aware of this. Now, what I'm more interested in is what happens after the military operation. Fighters go elsewhere to continue the military operation, but then in -- after when we have other soldiers that come about, or civilians, or paramilitaries, and this is when the problems occur. That's when the houses are torched, that's when there's rapes, looting, and so forth and so on. According to you, should the military commander also check what's happening after the operation, knowing that this kind of behaviour is probable? Isn't he supposed to secure the area, telling the military police to stay on site to make sure there will be no looting, no rapes, no crimes, or is the troop just marching on without really caring for what's happening behind them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question is a rather hypothetical one concerning while I was on duty. Well, we used to lose and regain or retake some positions, this hilltop, that hilltop, this elevation, that elevation. There were no operations such as the Neretva-92 operation, when we made progress. Combatants have their stints of combat duty of 15 days, 30 days, and when they're replaced they go home and cease to be soldiers. They have to respond to another mobilisation call-up. In the meantime, others replace them, and the same rules apply to them as well. A military commander does not occupy a certain territory. He's just responsible for the events at the front-line or, if he deems it necessary to do so, maybe behind the front-line because of infiltrating groups or such things. But military commanders cannot control the territory in depth. It is not their duty, and they are in no position, in terms of resources, to do so. For instance, in Rama, there were civilian authorities, the HVO, civilian police, civilian authorities, civilian structures, and they are supposed -- and now we are dealing with conditionals -- supposed to, depending on their mental state, to do such things. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me expound on this for the benefit of the President of the Chamber. When there's an order to close down cafes, to prohibit alcohol being served, then the civilian police were supposed to maintain law and order, or the military police was duty-bound to apprehend drunk people, et cetera, but it's not the duty of the military commander. They command their troops. Many things are clearly delineated in a military organisation, just as in the US Army. When there is an incident, military policemen will come and apprehend the perpetrators, and there is the appropriate procedure for them being punished, et cetera. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm very glad that we still have on the screen these provisions, Article 148 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which states who is duty-bound to file criminal reports. It says: "All government agencies, organisations of associated labour," et cetera, et cetera. In terms of criminal offences prosecuted ex officio, that they were informed of all that they learned about in other ways. You know about all this. Criminal offences is the subject matter, not the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said "a criminal report being filed." They report, and not a criminal report, because there's a legal difference between reporting and filing a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I do believe that there is no difference. There is only one criminal report as a notion. But let me deal with the matter of perpetrators unknown to see whether we've drawn an erroneous conclusion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, there's no mention of criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But paragraph 1, let's take a look at the heading, "Criminal Charge."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But to report on criminal offences does not mean to file criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's read. They report that a criminal offence is being committed. To the best of my understanding, this is not a criminal charge or a criminal report. You will allow me that I do know some law, myself. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I did not want Mr. Praljak to interpret law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise for having to intervene. We were revisiting this issue of interpreting law. I served as a judge for almost ten years applying this criminal procedure act. In Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia these were almost identical. This provision of Article 148 is not what should be done in terms of asking Mr. Praljak to give his answer. The ratio of this provision in the Criminal Procedure Act that we have to know in its entirety to be able to understand it was -- well, the law imposed a duty to a certain circle of persons who, if they learned that a criminal offence is being perpetrated, a criminal offence, indictable offence, or prosecutor ex officio, in other words, more severe form of criminal offence, they were duty-bound to report it. And the act of a reporting did not have a prescribed form or formal requirement. It was just a report. Somebody could pick up the phone and dial 9-1-1, Something has happened, send the police. The point of this Article is that certain entities or organisations or persons are duty-bound to do so. Why? Because in socialism, because of the constitutional guarantees and provisions, law may not have prescribed every citizen to be duty-bound to do so, as some other legal systems prescribe. So the lawmaker found the middle ground, accepting that not all citizens can be forced to report, but stating that at least the comrades listed here, who perform a responsible duty, as the law states, organs, organisations of associated labour and other entities, they are duty-bound to react because they are, in a way, part of the system of government. And that is the rationale for this. And now we cannot discuss who is duty-bound, the military or the civilians. And, of course, the second part of this story: I'm very saddened that I have to intervene. I do not feel proud. But such examination leads us nowhere. Mr. Praljak may be a perfect physician and starts examining me about nutrients, that would be a scene. I apologise, but I do believe that you have to understand that. At the very least, please hear my message. The rationale of this article is something completely different, and we cannot even discuss it. This debate, this discussion, is completely irrelevant. Thank you. And I apologise once again. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I believe that my learned friend misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You may have seen that I wanted to say something for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please sit down and calm down a bit. I would like the Chamber to be enlightened about the importance of the difference between what formerly is usually seen as a criminal report, which is a technical paper, which normally follows specific rules, or the criminal report in a broad, informal, untechnical sense, which is an information and which, it seems, is meant here. But where's the importance of that difference in the light of our proceedings? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may explain. This is my cross-examination. Your Honours, I do not see the problem, and I don't see the difference and whether this difference is relevant at all. I wanted to say what Mr. Kovacic said, that everybody was duty-bound --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There can be a difference, there really can be a difference, Counsel. I tried to understand what General Praljak was telling us. A brigade commander who has just been informed that a crime or an offence was committed, if he has any clues or any evidence at hand, then according to Article 27 he is duty-bound to seize the prosecutor. So he has to file a criminal report in due form. Now, on the other hand, and we're going to Article 148, if the brigade commander has little information or hardly any information, and he believes that this is not of his jurisdiction, he believes it's up to the investigating magistrate or the prosecutor to do something, then he can just report on this, just saying, This is what I heard, this is what I learned, I have no other element about this. So there he's just reporting the information. So, on the one hand, you can file a report, the brigade commander can file a report, and other -- or he can just signal, he can just report, he can say there were rumours. He can bring this to the attention of the authorities, of the competent authorities. I believe that this should be -- this can be interpreted, and this is actually how I would interpret Article 148. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given the fact that we've been talking this much about it, and I think we are disrupting my learned friend Dijana's cross-examination, which I do apologise for, given the fact that I was the person who authored the document that we have on our screens right now, and given the fact that I selected these four Articles from these two laws, if you deem it useful for us to know what the author of this document wanted to know, I can tell you in a couple of words. I wanted to compare a law that applies, in terms of criminal procedure, but before ordinary courts, as opposed to what applies before military courts. As for the Articles on page 1, I wanted to say this: For example, you have the Defence Ministry. Now, what does it need to do in relation to criminal offences that are prosecuted ex officio, in relation to an ordinary civilian criminal procedure? This applies before military courts in relation to military unit commanders. These Articles are comparable. What state organs do before ordinary civilian courts will be imposed as a special duty on a military commander before military courts. Page 2 shows a comparison between bodies whose task it is to track down the perpetrators of criminal offences, gather any information, and initiate criminal proceedings. The comparison is about this: Everything that civilian police do before civilian courts is exactly what authorised officials of the security organ do before military courts. The footnote clearly states, if you look at it, that under the provision of the Law on the Armed Forces, the security forces are the SIS and the military police. I think this is crystal clear, and I would be glad, indeed, for us all to finally understand this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to finish off this topic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it all started -- it all started for the following reason: I believed it was necessary, and I really can't go back to this now, to compare Article 151 with Article 27, paragraph 1 in both cases. They are identical, which is plain for all to see, with the following exception: Article 151 reads "track down the perpetrator of a criminal offence," whereas Article 27, the Decree on District Courts, does not contain that. And then I wanted to build upon that, what happens when a perpetrator remains unidentified. Whose duty is it then to track him down? And I was about to wrap it up. I would like to ask Ms. Alaburic -- she has just explained this for our benefit, and the Chamber can go ahead and read it themselves, is this actually in the documents or not, what I've just read out? Because how this comes across is the following: We all testify, Mr. Kovacic, Ms. Alaburic, and I do, when we are offering our legal opinions in terms of law and from the finer points of law, and I would really use this one example to try to explain what it's about --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first time around I did not intervene, and now I would like to say the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You forget the interpreters. You speak much too fast, and you start speaking long before the interpreter has been in a position to translate the previous sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first time 'round, when Ms. Tomic said that the provision of Article 151, paragraph 1, was identical to Article 27, paragraph 1, with the exception of tracking down the perpetrator, this was a misinterpretation, and the first time around I did not stand up to this, I did not oppose this. I will have to do this this time around, however. Article 151 contains another essential difference: Discover any evidence of a criminal offence or any items that might be used in evidence. Article 27 does not, in fact, comprise that. It merely reads that the duty is about preserving evidence. Therefore, something that is already there must be preserved. As for discovering evidence or discovering the perpetrator, any items that might be used in evidence, we only find that in Article 151. Claiming that these two legal provisions are identical is, in my opinion, tantamount to misleading those who are doing their best to understand the respective competences of the players in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, and I apologise to Ms. Tomic as well. This is my first interference, but I do believe that there is an interest of the Stojic Defence at stake here, in terms of clarifying this law. I would like to ask one thing, if at all possible, in the best interests of the Stojic Defence, for Ms. Tomic to be allowed to finish her cross-examination and for my other learned friends to refrain from legal interpretations. I have not witnessed anything like this in this courtroom, nor indeed have I done this myself. When Ms. Alaburic talked about the SIS annual reports, the word was recording she used, and the actual word was "discovery." I did not stand up to object, because I believed that the Chamber was in charge of reading these documents. They have the documents in front of them. What I would like to remind everyone at this juncture is: No one is to teach the Chamber about law. The Chamber has the documents right in front of them, and it is their duty to comment on these documents and interpret them. I think it would really be in order for us to allow our learned friends to press on with the cross-examination as envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic, as Ms. Nozica just said, you have to finish your cross-examination. You could have the floor. I think I understood that the point was to know who was competent when it comes to apprehending the perpetrator of a crime, if this perpetrator has not been identified. I think that's the crux of the matter. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Precisely, and I was just getting to that, I was building up to it. I would like to tell the Chamber one thing. I know this comes across as very inconvenient, and I do apologise to Mr. Praljak for making him face this situation, going through all these various situations with him and analysing them. That was not my original intention, nor indeed did I believe this would be the subject of his evidence, but eventually it did turn out to be the subject of his previous evidence. The Coric Defence will be bringing a witness somewhere down the line who will be qualified to tell us about the interpretation of these regulations, but I faced this situation. I had no choice at all. I had to see what Mr. Praljak actually knew about this. That was my intention. Mr. Praljak might as well tell me that he doesn't know, that he doesn't remember, or that he doesn't agree with me, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to answer this question by saying the following, and then I may as well be interrupted if I go wrong. In my interpretation, Article 27 and Article 151 are substantially different. I underline this. "To preserve" means that you already have something you're in possession of, something, and therefore you can preserve it. That's what Article 27 tells us. The word "to inform" in the Croatian language, at least, means I go in there and I say, Honourable Judges, I hereby inform you that this or that happened, and I have the body of evidence in my possession. That is the subject of a report. For example, the commander of a military unit should use that and preserve that. When he has it, he preserves it and informs others. In the other case, one must first find something or discover -- track down a perpetrator and discover any evidence available that was used in the commission of a crime. This is obvious even to a layman's eye. I tried to give the best evidence that I could based on my understanding of what a military commander, including me, was supposed to do in a situation like that. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, thank you very much. Let me give you a very simple example right now. Mr. Praljak, first I'll ask you this: Did you ever hear or did you know about the fact that a criminal report could be filed against an unknown perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Mr. Praljak, I'll give you an example in which a commander is aware of a crime that was committed but is unable to find a perpetrator because he finds no one there on the scene. For example, a commander comes across a house that was set ablaze and looted. At this point in time, he does not know who set fire to the house, whether it was soldiers or civilians. He just happens to stumble upon it, and there it is. Is my conclusion right, that regardless of all of this, he is duty-bound to preserve any evidence and inform the relevant prosecutor? I don't mean he, personally -- if he has any soldiers available they will do that for him, or an element of the military police, if he's not involved in the fighting, he comes across this house, his duty is to preserve any evidence and to inform the relevant prosecutor? Is that the meaning of Article 27?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If he comes across a house that was set ablaze, he has his own assistant for the SIS, he'll go up to him and say, Listen, lad, you're in charge of looking into that. He will probably go over there. He'll record all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he will inform the prosecutor; right? That is what Article 27 claims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He'll inform the prosecutor and he'll inform his own superior. He'll probably appeal for assistance and so on and so forth. This is the procedure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I really I cannot tolerate this anymore. I really do not understand. We have been asking you every time, every morning, every afternoon, to stop, in a proper way, and to listen to the questioning and then to answer. And I believe that actually everybody makes a mistake, this probably even myself, I do. But, on the other hand, it is really now we are torturing this very poor colleagues of ours, the interpreters, so I really don't understand why shouldn't have this empathy to act accordingly and to wait and to follow whatever is happening here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Prandler is very right. Please slow down. Unfortunately, we also are responsible, and given that we have very good interpreters and they can be very fast, and given that the Judges can understand very quickly, we can follow almost in realtime, despite the fact that we speak three different languages in this courtroom, but this is because we have very good interpreters. And despite that fact, you seem to go even faster because you have the feeling that you are speaking before Judges who speak your language, who come from your country, and you have the feeling that we understand you directly. And, indeed, sometimes we may understand things before you ask a question, but all the same, please slow down, because interpreters are subjected to tremendous efforts and sometimes they do send signals and they try to alert us. And we also have our court reporter, who is very good, but you can see that there are sometimes signs which show that he cannot really take down everything that is being said in this courtroom. So please slow down. I know that you are very passionate. Mr. Praljak talks, and the counsel then talk immediately after him, and things get heated up. So I suggest that we all calm down. We have 20 minutes to calm down, and we'll resume after 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to resume our hearing. Mr. Stringer, you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to inform the Trial Chamber and the parties that Exhibit P04494, which was the order from General Blaskic which had been poorly translated, the translation has been corrected, and we'll be uploading that in e-court as soon as the people can get that processed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Stringer. Ms. Tomic, you have the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Praljak, the last thing we stated was that a criminal report could, indeed, be filed against an unknown perpetrator. Can we now please go to 4D01105. This is the Law on Criminal Procedure. Can we please go to Article 153, paragraph 2, of that law?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, have you got that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. It reads: "If a public prosecutor cannot conclude, based on the report itself, whether the allegations contained in the report are plausible, or if information contained in the report does not provide sufficient basis to decide whether to launch an investigation or not, or if the only thing that reached the public prosecutor was a rumour to the effect that a criminal offence was committed, and particularly if there is an unknown perpetrator involved, the public prosecutor shall, unless unable to take action himself or through other bodies, request bodies of the Ministry of the Interior to gather necessary information and take any other measures that are required to uncover a crime or track down a perpetrator. The public prosecutor may at all times request any bodies of the Ministry of the Interior any measures taken." Before I ask you my next question, I would like to go to Article 155. It's on the same page. It reads: "When the perpetrator of a criminal offence is unidentified, the public prosecutor may request for a body of the Ministry of the Interior to take investigative action if, in relation to the circumstances of a case, it deems necessary to take any such action even before an investigation is launched. If the public prosecutor believes that certain investigative steps must be taken by investigating judge or, indeed, if there is a post-mortem or an exhumation to be performed, he shall make a proposal to the investigative judge to take such action. If the investigative judge does not agree with that proposal, he will be requesting a decision of the chamber." Mr. Praljak, why am I showing you these two Articles? The reason is to ascertain what happens when we are dealing with an unknown perpetrator, and when a prosecutor has been informed of a crime but the perpetrator remains unknown. It follows from this that he should then get other bodies to prosecute this. In this case, it is the MUP, and in case of the military courts, it would be the security bodies of the armed forces, meaning the military police and the SIS. Mr. Praljak, were you aware of the fact that the procedure was as described here? Did you know that this was what went on, and did you know that these were the Articles being applied, describing what the appropriate course of action would have been in terms of who got involved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the best part of all of this; not down to the minutest detail, but I did know that investigative bodies, such as the prosecutor and the investigative judge, had certain powers, and that is precisely what it says. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will try to conclude this subject with the last document in this binder, P06137. This is an order by Mr. Petkovic, dated the 26th of October, 1993, titled "The Implementation of an Investigative Procedure." I will briefly read the order. It was addressed to the commander of Operations Group 2, Central Bosnia Operational District, Mr. Ivica Rajic, as well as to the commander of the Bobovac Brigade in Vares, Mr. Emil Harah. I'll start reading from paragraph 2, which reads: "A powerful media campaign is being waged on BH Radio and Television against Vares and Kakanj-based HVO units. "They are being accused of abusing the civilian population, torching family homes and businesses. In this way, attempts are being made to tarnish the reputation of HVO units. In the interests of establishing a situation that occurred after and during combat in this Stupni Do sector and pursuant to Article 59 of the Rules of Military Discipline, I hereby order: "1. Conduct a complete investigation into the aforesaid event and, in particular: A, which units and which commanders participated in combat tasks; B, in what way was the area of the village of Stupni Do taken; C, how the civilian population of Stupni Do village treated if there were any civilians found in the area; D, in what state were residential and business buildings found, and what was done with them after the area was taken; E, did any HVO members behave in contravention of regulations, tarnishing the reputation of HVO units, and if there was any such behaviour, the perpetrators should be identified." Paragraph 2: "In the course of the investigation, involve without fail the competent organs and work constantly with them until a light has been shed on all the circumstances that arose after the village of Stupni Do was taken." Paragraph 3: "After the completion of the investigation, submit a written report and full documentation on the investigation, as well as any findings by the competent organs, by the 15th of November, 1993, at the latest." Paragraph 4: "The following commanders [as interpreted] shall be directly responsible to me for implementation of this order." Mr. Praljak, what I wish to ask you is the following. I have two questions for you. I'll put them both together, and then you can answer both at the same time. My first question: Based on this order, does it not follow that the only thing that reached the commander issuing the order through the media was a mere rumour that something or other might have happened somewhere; nevertheless, at the time he issued this order, he was not in possession of any other information regarding that? My other question: Is this the way a responsible commander would act, in keeping with Article 59 of the Rules of Military Discipline and in keeping with everything else that we have witnessed so far in the course of this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your first question, I advise you to look closely at what General Petkovic is writing here, in terms of how he found out about this. In response to your other question, these are exactly the steps that a responsible commander would take. At his own level, he requests that military commanders submit information that he would then be including in a report forwarding to the relevant bodies in charge of the investigation. That's perfectly clear. This is exactly what a responsible commander is supposed to do; seek information and involve any relevant bodies. He will be forwarding information to them, and they will go on working together on this. He requests a written report to be submitted on this, as well as an opinion from the relevant bodies, who will then go on and establish the final truth on an event that occurred. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: Thank you very much, Mr. Praljak. All right, I'm done with this subject. I was about to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A correction to the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 87, line 4, I think it reads "the following commanders," but in fact it's "the above" and not "the following." MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Croatian reads "those mentioned." I think that boils down to the same thing that you said, but it reads "those mentioned."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And this translation is "the above," but it's the opposite to the following, and nothing follows, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, now the counsel has concluded her questioning, I have some follow-up questions to ask you regarding this document. The first one is the following. I would like to know why you were not the one to issue this order. Why was it General Petkovic, who was number two, who signed this order? Why did you not sign this order yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, for several reasons. First of all, I command General Petkovic, and he commands everybody else except for me. He's my deputy, and his orders are executive unless I rescind them. This is the first point. He's number two and is entitled to issue orders to everybody except to me. The second point. General Petkovic was in Kiseljak at the time. He was closer to the events. He was up there, he was close to the events, to the venue, and it would be only logical and normal for him to request an investigation, being there, and he would be quicker to receive any information than I, who was 200 kilometres away as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Second question. In a military setting, this type of request is what we call a command investigation. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He orders that the military structures collect all the information; who was there, who were the commanders, what they knew, to receive information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In a command investigation, where the higher authorities want to be informed of what happened, as far as you're concerned, do you think it was advisable to ask Mr. Rajic and Mr. Harah to launch their own investigation or to carry out their own investigation while they were a party to what happened, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Antonetti, he says here, Those who were there, there are no others, will provide me with the information about the facts, but the competent organs should be involved, and the competent organs will carry out an investigation in a broader circle of people, other than those who may be involved in the 19 mistreatment in Stupni Do. These are two levels. He will provide these 20 competent organs with the information that he could get from the people who 21 were there. But this is not a closed set of information. If they want to 22 prevent disclosure of some information, then the responsible persons, as him, 23 would involve SIS, the military police, and he cannot skip them. They have 24 to give their information about what happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2 of this order, I can see that the relevant authorities had to be informed of this investigation. I was wondering whether the military prosecutor also had to carry out its own investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what it means: Military will carry out an investigation. This, what is described, is only support to the military investigator so that he may get to the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This order is dated 26th of October, 1993. Did you learn immediately that Mr. Petkovic had asked an investigation to be carried out by a Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that Mr. Petkovic demanded an investigation to be made, and we at the Main Staff -- I believe I was the one who signed it, or Tole. But upon learning about this, we demanded as well that an investigation be carried out, and that document has been shown here, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But given the text of the former JNA, and even if you look at the text of the ABiH or the HVO, usually when you have a military operation, don't you have to also include at some stage the military police? In the orders that are issued, don't you always also bring on board the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. In any military operation, the military police have their duties to perform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as regards General Petkovic or yourself, when there were some rumours that were going around stating that something may have happened in this town, as it is mentioned in the document, because it says there has been a media campaign, I was wondering whether you didn't ask yourself what the military police did. Were they there, what did they do, or you actually didn't ask yourself this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked myself all of these things, but you have to conduct an investigation to get to the facts who did what, to which extent. You have my orders, you saw them, demanding that procedures be stepped up and accelerated, everything that could be done under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this operation regarding this village, which was an intricate operation to carry it out because you needed to have the agreement of the Serbs in order to cross their lines, so it was not a small military operation, in this type of operation I was wondering whether you shouldn't have included the military police from the outset.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not an extensive military operation, Your Honour. Some 30-odd members of the Army of BiH defended that village. But irrespective of what the extent was, military police is usually involved in military operations and has a role to play in military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well, except that in this very example, they were not part of the military operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, but it is equally correct, Your Honours - I don't know how many times do I have to reiterate - the communication between Vares and the Main Staff were simply to the effect that information received through packet communication -- well, I don't know how to reply. This was an enclave encircled on one side by the Serbs, being attacked on the other side by the Army of BiH. I could work on or act on information at my disposal. When I received the information about disorder, I reacted by demanding that merciless action should be taken to bring HVO ranks back to order, and I requested from General Petkovic, not as an order but as a request, that these had to be removed, but unfortunately that came in too late, at least with respect to Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were not involved, you mentioned this, for Ahmici, but you had heard about what had happened in Ahmici. And when you realised that in Stupni Do the same type of events may have occurred, did you not realise at that stage that you should, yourself, go on the ground in order to display the fullest degree of transparency because you knew that the international community would look at this very closely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic is a highly-educated officer. He enjoyed my full support and my full trust, as my deputy, and I had no reason to believe that he would not carry out all the duties and all the steps as if I were there. The second thing. It was not an easy task to get there. Petkovic reached that area via either an UNPROFOR helicopter or an UNPROFOR APC. You couldn't just simply take a vehicle and go to Vares. It had to be organised 10 to 15 days in advance, if it was successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will now give the floor to Ms. Tomic. I'm sure she'll move to the third binder now. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're putting the binder into place, Mr. Praljak, by way of an introduction, I'm going to ask you this: So far you've discussed that military police took part in combat operations, as far as I could understand you. You said that in the case of combat operations, military police was under operational command of the commander in charge of the operation in question. And when we talk about combat operations of that kind, we mean and we say that military policemen would be fighting at the front-line, just like any other troops, and perform tasks as given. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there, I received such powers that, in operational terms, military police units would be my subordinates, in operational terms, which means that they were still military policemen when they were not engaged in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Praljak, apart from being involved in military operations or combat operations, the military police had to perform their everyday military police duties; to man check-points, fight crime. Can we agree that these would be everyday tasks of the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, daily tasks of brigade military police and those serving in an operation zone or area. And let me not repeat all the tasks that I've already mentioned. And, of course, the military police had all those other duties that you mentioned. This is not contentious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's put aside brigade military police and not deal with it. Let's deal with the military police battalion within an operations zone. I do not mean the light assault battalion, whose priority task was a combat one, but your regular military police within an operations zone. They, too, have their everyday military police tasks to perform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct; to provide security, to provide sentry duty for their headquarters of the operation zone, command, but not too many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it have any other task?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe to guard a warehouse, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it also have tasks concerning check-points and crime?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. These are not everyday -- oh, I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military police tasks, let me put it this way, one of the everyday tasks would be what they're issued every day as tasks to perform within their military police work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I've repeatedly shown in this courtroom, and I failed to prepare this because you said that you did not deal with structures specifically. Those documents have been adduced into evidence. You don't have them in the binder. I can now show it to everybody subsequently, but I believe that you will recall what I'm talking about. The document in question is the structure of the military police of the HVO from December 1992, which is -- which entered into force in January 1993, and prepared by Mr. Coric. That would be P00957. Mr. Praljak, please tell us, in that document, it is stated - and you will tell us whether you knew about that - that commanders of military police battalions within operation zones, in performing their everyday tasks, would be immediately subordinated to the commander of the operations zone and would carry out all orders concerning the execution of military police tasks and are in compliance with the purview and authorities and powers of the military police. I can give you this document as a print-out. It is not essential to me whether you knew what was written in that document, but whether you knew that this was so and that it functioned in this way.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should read it first. To be fair, I think it somehow slipped my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see on e-court the last page of the document, the penultimate paragraph, so we can all read it. It is stated that the Military Police Administration manages and commands all military police units, and then there is text describing everyday tasks of the military police, the penultimate paragraph, the one that I just read out.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with that? Do you know other commanders were informed of that, and whether they really issued orders for daily duties which the military policemen had to perform the way that it is stated here in this document, and whether this mechanism functioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a two-pronged test. Military commanders could issue orders in the execution of military-police tasks pursuant to the powers and responsibilities of military police. Therefore, they could do their job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. Praljak. I did not want to state anything different from that. You know why I showed you this document? Because on several occasions you stated today that commanders had to seek special permission from the Military Police Administration - I apologise, I'm speaking too fast - to be able to issue such duties as we see described here, and I just want to remind you that there was no need for any special orders when this was regulated by a general document entitling them to do so. This was my sole intention in showing you this document. And I repeat that these are daily duties of the military police. I'm not discussing combat operation duties of military police.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall saying that they had to seek special dispensation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
