utterances.text: I do not recall saying that they had to seek permission from anybody to issue orders to military police to do their job, if they were not doing their job already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Praljak. I was afraid that this is being misunderstood, and this is why I wanted to clarify that. In the third binder, the last binder, let us take a look at some documents which I believe will demonstrate what the execution of everyday military police tasks is, and how orders are issued, and how this whole thing functions. We will start with this first document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'm still looking at the previous document, and I have questions about the last paragraph of this document. Mr. Stojic and Mr. Coric seem to say that the military police battalions present in the operational zones are directly subordinated to the commander of the zone, so in this document it says that when there is a military action underway, the military police battalions are directly subordinated or depend directly on the commander of the operational zone. This connection which exists between the battalion and the operation zone commander, I would like to know whether this coordination could go all the way to investigation, or it just means that they can be involved in combat? If it means that they should be involved in combat, doesn't that risk to jeopardise the commander of the brigade, because he's executing the orders of the operations zone commander, but in combat he's supposed to be in total command of his troops? So how can you -- how can this fit in with what should happen and what actually happened on the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until the point in time when the situation on the battle-field became very bad for the HVO, and that was even prior to my arrival and at the time of my arrival, the military police had not been involved in any military or combat operations. I then sought and received those powers. As of such a time, a commander, me or anyone else, was in a position to use military police on a combat mission. Otherwise, we would simply have been defeated by the BH Army. It's as simple as that. Had I not received those powers, I would never have taken over my role as commander of the Main Staff. It's that simple, really. Among the military policemen, the military police battalions and light assault battalions, there were some extraordinarily brave, well-trained lads who fought well. Prior to that period, however, and when they were away from the front-line, they were still military policemen structurally linked to the chief of the military police, performing all of their tasks which they were supposed to perform by virtue of being military policemen, unlike what we might term an ordinary soldier; once his own stint at the front-line was over, he would be away on leave and go home until he was called again. Military police officers never went home. They were professional units, and they would sleep in compounds when they were not somewhere along the front-line, going about their own work, because it was their duty or else a zone commander was in possession of some special information on something or other, and then he would say, Please investigate this or that because something happened, there was a brawl over there, something or other was stolen. And then they would go out and do it. It's perfectly simple. There is nothing complicated about that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, in the -- according to the theory of the military police, and you -- Mr. Coric is a specialist in that because he had some role in the military police, so according to the case of the military police, military police battalions are subordinated to the highest-ranking officials at the Ministry of Defence. We can understand that. But we have this document which has been signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Coric, and it changes the situation slightly, stating that when there is an operations zone, so when you have an operation on the ground, the military police will be directly subordinated -- it says directly subordinated to the operations zone commander, that's what it says in English, which means that Mr. Coric and Mr. Stojic may well say that when you carry out a military operation, We are too far away from the front-line, it is up to the operations zone commander to take charge of the military police control. Otherwise, why would there be this sentence in this document? What's your take on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, I'll repeat this. One thing is when they go on a mission, they receive their military assignment, You're to cover this or that territory, We'll be taking over this line or that hill, You'll take back this hill or that hill lost to the enemy by someone or other three days before. That's one thing. The other job would entail the powers and competences of the military police, because they have both, the powers and competences and duties. This is something that the military police must perform. Nevertheless, the commander has every right to point this out to them in case he knows something about this. Back to your question. For example, you happen to see some houses that were on fire. You would then go back to the military police and the SIS, the assistant for the SIS, to try and investigate how that came about. These are the powers and competences of the military police, and he has every right to ask them to do this. On the other hand, the commander of that battalion also has the duty to take this action himself, as well as a number of other steps, some of them daily, such as protecting a convoy, or escorting a UN convoy, for example, or a military convoy, an HVO convoy, or indeed block a road leading to the front-line in order to prevent someone approaching the soldiers along the front-line from the rear. There were daily tasks, practical tasks, such as these. There were other tasks, too, stemming from their powers and competences. Those were specifically defined, the powers and competences, I mean, in military police documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, and then I want to give the floor back to the counsel. I believe you know this more than anybody else. When there is a military operation, it is very likely that some prisoners will be taken, and those prisoners will be apprehended and watched over by the military police. And if they are under their custody for a while, it is very likely that during that period it will be the military police that will be in charge of that. But if there is a document, such as the one we have before us, which states that they are directly subordinated to the operations zone commander, as far as you are concerned regarding the prisoners, who has authority, the operations zone commander, because of this document, or will it go to higher authorities such as Mr. Coric or Mr. Stojic, when dealing with logistical issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not the military police that necessarily captures prisoners of war. Any HVO soldier may capture a prisoner of war, or indeed a military police officer who happened to be involved in an operation where someone simply surrendered to them. The moment a POW surrenders to the military police, the operations zone brigade commander’s concern about these POWs ceases. At this point in time, they are handed over to whichever relevant body is in charge of looking after these POWs from there on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what would be this relevant body in our case here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of the military police, the Security Service, the prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that we are looking at a core issue here. If you have what I would call military prisoners from the ABiH, so they are military prisoners, and if I understood you correctly, you said that the role of the military police will stop there and they have to be handed over to the relevant body. I asked you what is the relevant body, and you tell me the chief of the military police, the Security Service, or the SIS, or the prisons .

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not "or," I didn't say "or." The moment POWs are taken charge of by the military police, the military commander is no longer in charge of those prisoners. That's what I said. They are then taken to prison, no alternative, probably to be interrogated by the SIS. I won't speculate on this. But a prisoner that is handed over to the military police is no longer in the charge of the military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I think that your answer is crystal clear. According to you, as soon as you have military prisoners or prisoners of war, the brigade commander is no longer the relevant authority. You have reiterated that at several instances, so we will have that in mind. Counsel Tomic, I do not know how much you've got left, but we only have a few minutes left for today. The Registrar tells me that you have used two hours and nine minutes, which means that, in theory, you have a further two hours and thirty-six minutes, since you had four hours and forty-five minutes to start with, which means that if there is no objection, no incident, you should be able to conclude tomorrow. Were you planning to conclude tomorrow, Ms. Tomic? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is very difficult for me to plan. I think it doesn't really depend on me, and we could see that today. There is so much going on in this courtroom. I'm understandably not fully in control of the situation as to how long my cross-examination will take. I can tell you how much time my questions will take. As to anything else that might go on in the courtroom tomorrow, I really can't say. Anyway, I think there is too little time left for me to embark on a new document. That's best left for tomorrow, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. A point of clarification, Counsel, because as far as I was concerned it was clear, but there might be some doubt. You had four hours. I thought that you had asked, like the other teams, four hours and forty-five minutes. So the total should be four hours and forty-five minutes or is it four hours? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, four hours and forty-five minutes. I did say at the outset, when I started cross-examining, and that was granted by you, that if I failed to deal with everything in the four hours and forty-five minutes allotted, whether I would be given the right to use Mr. Coric's Defence time, and that was granted me at the beginning of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there was some delays linked to objections, as things stand, are you still on target and are you still planning to conclude in four hours and forty-five minutes? Because as I said to you, you will have two hours and thirty-six minutes to conclude tomorrow. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way things are going, and if I manage to work according to plan, if documents are found at the rate I envisage, then I will be able to finish within the four hours and forty-six minutes, but it's difficult to predict. Sometimes General Praljak's answer is lengthier than I expect. It's very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will have to leave this courtroom, because in less than 25 minutes I will be in another trial. So I wish you a very good afternoon, and we'll meet again here at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
